readmes.dev.yabbistir.dev-servers:
# Dev Servers

The local servers listening on your Mac, as a column in yabbistir's panel, found with `lsof`. Each row shows the program and its port (`node · 3000`) and, quieter, its process id and address (`pid 4100 · 127.0.0.1`). ↵ pastes `http://localhost:3000`, ⇧↵ pastes `localhost:3000`, and ⌘C copies the link.

## Example

You started a Vite server and forgot its port. Open the panel, move to the *Dev servers* column, type `vite` and press ↵: `http://localhost:5173` is pasted.

A program that listens on both IPv4 and IPv6 (`127.0.0.1` and `::1`) on the same port is one row, with both addresses in the subtitle. A listener on every interface shows *all interfaces*. Two processes on one port (a server and its workers) are two rows.

## Setup

None. `lsof` ships with macOS.

## Stopping a server

The extension does not stop processes. A source action cannot ask for confirmation first, and ending a process on a single keypress is too easy to do by mistake. So ⇧↵ pastes `localhost:<port>`, and you stop a server yourself in Terminal, with the pid from the row's subtitle:

```sh
kill 4100
```

`kill` sends SIGTERM, which lets the program shut down cleanly. Use `kill -9` only when it does not.

## Permissions and privacy

- **exec**, limited to `lsof`. The extension runs `lsof -nP +c 0 -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -F pcun`, always with these fixed options and no row content. It reads each listening process's name, process id, user id and local address and port. It asks for no network permission and runs no other tool.
- **Only your own processes.** lsof run without `sudo` lists only what you may see, which is your own programs. Processes of root (user id 0) are left out as well.
- **Nothing is kept.** The list is read each time the panel opens, lives in the app's memory, and never reaches the history, a file or a log. A row's id (`<pid>-<port>`) is checked before it becomes a paste.

## Limits

- Only TCP listeners; UDP and Unix sockets are not shown.
- Command names come from lsof as the system reports them; a program that renames itself shows its new name.
- A server may stop between the list and the paste: the link is pasted anyway.
- Programs of macOS itself that run as you (for example Control Center or rapportd) listen on ports too and appear as rows; only root-owned listeners are hidden.
- `lsof` ships with macOS, so the manifest's install note is a sentence rather than a `brew` command.
- Another user's processes that you can see (for example in a shared machine) are not told apart from yours.
readmes.dev.yabbistir.browser-tabs:
# Browser Tabs

Your open browser tabs as a column in yabbistir's panel, so you can paste a link to one without switching to the browser. It works with Safari, Google Chrome, Arc, Brave, Microsoft Edge and Vivaldi. Each row shows the tab's title, with the browser and the site's host under it. ↵ pastes the tab's link, ⇧↵ pastes it as a Markdown link, and ⌘C copies the link.

## Example

You are writing in Slack and want to share the pull request open in Chrome. Open the panel, move to the *Open tabs* column and type `pull`. The row *Pull request #42* (`Chrome · code.example.org`) is there:

- ↵ pastes `https://code.example.org/pull/42`
- ⇧↵ pastes `[Pull request #42](https://code.example.org/pull/42)`

## Order

The tab you are looking at in each window comes first: the active tab of every window, then the other tabs. Within that, the browser in front comes first, then Safari, Chrome, Arc, Brave, Edge and Vivaldi, with each browser's windows from front to back and the tabs in their order. Blank pages, new tab pages and start pages (Vivaldi's included) are left out, since they have nothing to link to.

## Setup

None to install. The column asks only the browsers that are already open.

The first time the column reads a browser, macOS asks whether yabbistir may control it ("“yabbistir” wants access to control “Safari”…"). Allow it once for each browser you use. If you answer after a few seconds, the column may say it couldn't read the tabs that time; open the panel again.

If you chose *Don’t Allow*, the column shows one row that says where to change it: **System Settings › Privacy & Security › Automation**, where you turn on the browser's switch under yabbistir. When only some browsers are allowed, the others' tabs are listed and a row at the end names the browser that isn't.

## Private windows

Private windows are left out where the browser says which windows are private: Chrome, Brave, Edge and Vivaldi (incognito and InPrivate windows, from the window's `mode`) and Arc (from the window's `incognito`). A window in these browsers that doesn't answer whether it is private is left out too, so a private window's tabs are never listed by mistake; if that leaves nothing to show, the column says it couldn't read the tabs. Safari's scripting does not tell private windows apart, so **Safari's private windows are listed like any other**.

## Permissions and privacy

- **exec**, limited to `osascript`, which comes with macOS. The extension runs one fixed script with `osascript -l JavaScript -e <script>`. The script is part of the extension: it is never built from a tab, a row or anything you copied. It takes at most one argument, the browser to read, one of six fixed words (`safari`, `chrome`, `arc`, `brave`, `edge`, `vivaldi`): listing the column passes none and reads every browser, and ↵, ⇧↵ or ⌘C passes the tab's browser so only that one is asked again. It only reads: for each browser that is running, its windows' ids and whether they are private, and its tabs' ids, titles and addresses. It never opens, closes or changes a tab, never runs JavaScript in a page, and never asks a browser that isn't already running.
- **Why osascript:** browsers share their tabs with other apps only through Apple events, and osascript is how a program sends them. The store's review checklist counts osascript among the shells, since a script can do anything; here the script is fixed, so the review is of that one script, in [`src/script.ts`](src/script.ts).
- **Automation.** macOS asks you before yabbistir controls each browser, and you can turn that off at any time in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Automation.
- **Nothing is kept.** The tabs are read each time you open the panel, and the tab's browser again when you press ↵, ⇧↵ or ⌘C, so the link pasted is the one the tab has now. The extension keeps no tab in its storage, in a file or in its memory, and never writes a title or an address to the log or into an error message. yabbistir keeps the rows in memory only, never in its history, its search index or on disk, and a link it pastes from the column does not enter the history either.
- **Only the host is shown.** A row's second line shows the browser and the site's host (`example.com`), never the rest of the address, so a token in a link's query stays out of sight. The full address is what ↵ pastes.
- No network permission: the extension itself reaches nothing outside your Mac.

## Markdown links

⇧↵ pastes `[Title](address)`. In the title, `\ [ ] < > * _` and `` ` `` are escaped with a backslash, so the title shows as written; in the address, spaces, `<`, `>` and parentheses are percent-encoded so the link does not end early. A tab without a title links with its host.

## Limits

- **Browsers:** Safari, Google Chrome, Arc, Brave, Microsoft Edge and Vivaldi, the release versions. Firefox shares no tabs through Apple events. Beta and Canary channels, Chromium, Opera and Safari Technology Preview are not asked.
- **Arc:** Little Arc windows have no scripting, so their tabs are not listed.
- **Many tabs:** each browser answers a few Apple events per window, not one per tab, so hundreds of tabs read quickly. The column shows up to 10,000 tabs, the active ones first.
- **A busy browser:** a browser that does not answer within the panel's 10 seconds keeps the whole column from loading that time. Pasting asks only the tab's own browser, so a busy Arc never holds up a link from Chrome or Safari.
- **Rows follow tabs:** a tab's row stays the same while it is open. Safari gives tabs no id, so a Safari row follows the tab's window and address: opening, closing or moving other tabs leaves it alone, but when the tab goes to another page or into another window, its row is a new one. Two Safari tabs with the same address in one window are told apart by their order, so closing the first of them changes the second one's row. If you press ↵ on a row whose tab has since changed or closed, the column says the tab is no longer open.

## Sources

- Chromium's scripting dictionary, shared by Chrome, Brave, Edge and Vivaldi: [`scripting.sdef`](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/refs/heads/main/chrome/browser/ui/cocoa/applescript/scripting.sdef), and the window modes `normal` and `incognito` in [`constants_applescript.mm`](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/chrome/browser/ui/cocoa/applescript/constants_applescript.mm).
- Arc's scripting: [Arc AppleScript API](https://browserinc.notion.site/Arc-AppleScript-API-897272210c784627ba3925a7610b02b6), and the dictionary Arc 1.153.1 ships (Script Editor › File › Open Dictionary › Arc): a window's `id`, `incognito` and `active tab`, and a tab's `id`, `title` and `URL`.
- Safari's scripting: the dictionary Safari 26.6 ships (Script Editor › File › Open Dictionary › Safari): a window's `current tab`, and a tab's `name`, `URL` and `visible`.
- How osascript hands the script its argument: the `osascript(1)` manual page ("Any arguments following the script will be passed as a list of strings to the direct parameter of the run handler").
- JavaScript for Automation, `Application(bundleID)` and `running()`: Apple's JXA release notes for [OS X 10.10](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/releasenotes/InterapplicationCommunication/RN-JavaScriptForAutomation/Articles/OSX10-10.html) and [OS X 10.11](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/releasenotes/InterapplicationCommunication/RN-JavaScriptForAutomation/Articles/OSX10-11.html).
- What macOS answers when Automation is off, "Not authorized to send Apple events to …" (-1743): [Avoiding AppleScript security and privacy requests](https://scriptingosx.com/2020/09/avoiding-applescript-security-and-privacy-requests/), Scripting OS X.
- Safari's dictionary has no private-window property: [Using AppleScript to detect if a Safari window uses Private Browsing](https://alexwlchan.net/2021/detect-private-browsing/), alexwlchan.

# Fake Data

Makes fake data for forms, fixtures and demos. Search for what you need (`fake`, `iban`, `tckn`, `email`, `lorem`) and press ↵: the value is pasted, and the row shows it before you pick it.

- **Fake person:** full name, first name, last name, username, date of birth (an adult, 18 to 80 years old, as `YYYY-MM-DD`).
- **Fake contact:** email, phone number, street address, city.
- **Fake work details:** company, job title.
- **Fake number:** Turkish ID number (TCKN), Turkish tax number (VKN), Turkish IBAN, and test card numbers (Visa, Mastercard, American Express).
- **Lorem ipsum:** a sentence or a paragraph.
- **Fake user (JSON):** one made-up person as a JSON object: id, name, email, username, phone, date of birth, company, job title and address. With Turkish data it has a `tckn` and an `iban` too.

## Example

```json
{
  "id": "5c1f0e0a-3a66-4a4f-9a0e-0d7f2a5a9b11",
  "firstName": "Elif",
  "lastName": "Kaya",
  "email": "elif.kaya@example.org",
  "username": "ekaya42",
  "phone": "+90 532 418 07 26",
  "birthDate": "1991-06-14",
  "company": "Mavi Yazılım A.Ş.",
  "jobTitle": "Ürün Yöneticisi",
  "address": { "street": "Gül Sokak No: 14/3", "city": "İzmir" },
  "tckn": "10000000146",
  "iban": "TR330006100519786457841326"
}
```

## Language of the data

Settings has one choice, **Language of the data**: *Same as the app* (the default), *Turkish* or *English*. It changes names, cities, streets, companies, job titles and phone formats. The Turkish ID, tax number and IBAN are always Turkish, and the card numbers and lorem ipsum never change.

## What is real and what is not

This data is fake. **Never use it to pretend to be someone, or for real payments.**

- **Names, cities, streets, companies, job titles** come from short lists written for this extension from common words. No list was taken from a real record. Because the lists are short and common, a made-up name can match a real person by chance.
- **Email** always ends in `example.com`, `example.org` or `example.net`, the names RFC 2606 reserves for documentation and tests. Mail to them reaches no one.
- **Phone numbers:** English numbers are US style (`+1 (area) 555-01xx`); there is no UK style. They use `555-0100` to `555-0199`, the range set aside for fiction. Turkey has no such range, so a Turkish mobile number is random and may belong to someone. Use it only to fill a field, never to call or send a message.
- **TCKN, VKN and IBAN** pass the public check-digit rules, so form validators accept them. They are random: a number may happen to belong to a real person or account. The IBAN is pasted compact, without spaces (`TR33…`), which is what forms usually want. Its five-digit bank code is picked from a short list of codes in the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye's published bank list; the account number is random and opens nothing.
- **Test cards** are the numbers the card networks publish for testing (`4111 1111 1111 1111` Visa, `5555 5555 5555 4444` Mastercard, `3782 822463 10005` American Express). They pass the Luhn check, work in the networks' test modes, and never belong to a real account. There is no expiry or security code: test systems take any future date and any code.
- **Lorem ipsum** uses the classic Latin placeholder words, which are in the public domain.

Everything is made on your Mac from `crypto.getRandomValues`, with no network.

## Permissions and tools

None. The extension needs no permission, runs no program and makes no request.

## Limits

- Each row makes one value; pick the row again for a new one.
- Turkish and English only.
- Data is meant to look plausible, not to be statistically realistic.

# Authenticator

Your two-factor codes as a column in yabbistir's panel, computed on your Mac. You export your accounts from your authenticator app once and paste the export into the extension's settings, where it is kept in the Keychain. Each row shows a service and the account name; ↵ pastes the current code into the field you are in.

It works with any authenticator that exports its accounts:

- **otpauth:// links**, one or many: Ente Auth, Aegis's text export and many other apps write lists of these.
- **LastPass Authenticator**: its file export.
- **Google Authenticator**: the `otpauth-migration://` links in its export QR codes.
- **Aegis**: its unencrypted JSON export.
- **2FAS**: its `.2fas` backup without a password.
- **Bitwarden Authenticator**: its JSON or CSV export (a Bitwarden Password Manager JSON export works too).
- **2FAuth**: its JSON migration file.

The format is recognized on its own, and several can go into the field together, such as a few otpauth links and a Google export.

## Example

You are signing in to *ornek.dev* and it asks for a code. Open the panel and move to the *Authenticator* column, type `ornek` to find *ornek.dev* (`deniz@ornek.dev`) and press ↵: the six digits are pasted. When fewer than three seconds of the code's 30 seconds are left, the next code is pasted instead, which most sites accept a few seconds early.

## Setup

1. Export your accounts from your authenticator app, as below.
2. Open the export and copy all of it. In yabbistir, go to Settings › Extensions › Authenticator, paste it into **Accounts** and press Save.
3. Delete the copy from yabbistir's history right away: select it in the panel and press ⌘⌫.
4. Open the *Authenticator* column and check that it lists every account. If some are missing from a list of links, put the links on one line, separated by spaces, and paste again.
5. Only then delete the export: the file, the Trash, the file on your phone, and any photos of QR codes. See [Keeping the export safe](#keeping-the-export-safe).

To add accounts later, export again: press Clear next to Accounts, paste the new export and press Save.

## Exporting your accounts

### LastPass Authenticator

1. On your phone, open LastPass Authenticator and go to Settings › Transfer accounts › **Export accounts to file**.
2. Save the file and move it to your Mac, with AirDrop for example.
3. Open it with TextEdit, then select all and copy it (⌘A, ⌘C).

The QR codes of *Export accounts to QR code* are not read: pasting one makes the column say so. Use the file.

### Google Authenticator

1. In Google Authenticator, open the menu and go to Transfer accounts › **Export accounts**, choose the accounts and tap Next. It shows one QR code, or several when you export many accounts.
2. Read the text in each QR code: it starts with `otpauth-migration://offline?data=`. Any QR reader that shows the text instead of opening it works. On the Mac, take a screenshot or a photo of each code (Google Authenticator may block screenshots; a photo from another device works), then read them all in Terminal with [zbar](https://github.com/mchehab/zbar):

   ```sh
   brew install zbar
   zbarimg --raw -q code1.jpg code2.jpg
   ```

3. Copy every line it prints, all the codes together. They can be on separate lines or separated by spaces.
4. Afterwards, delete the photos or screenshots from your phone too, empty *Recently Deleted* in Photos, and clear Terminal with ⌘K: its scrollback still holds the links.

### Aegis

1. In Aegis, go to Settings › Import & Export › **Export**.
2. Choose *Aegis (.JSON)* or *Text file (.TXT)*, and turn off *Encrypt the vault*. The text file is much smaller, since the JSON carries your icons: take it for a large vault.
3. Move the file to your Mac, open it with TextEdit and copy all of it.

### 2FAS

1. In 2FAS, go to Settings › 2FAS Backup › **Export**.
2. Turn off the password option and tap *Export to file*.
3. Move the `.2fas` file to your Mac, open it with TextEdit and copy all of it.

### Bitwarden Authenticator

1. In Bitwarden Authenticator, go to Settings › **Export** and choose `.json` (or `.csv`).
2. Move the file to your Mac, open it with TextEdit and copy all of it.

Only codes stored in the Authenticator app are in its export. Codes kept in your Bitwarden vault come with a vault export instead, which must be unencrypted (a *.json* export, not *.json (Encrypted)*).

### Ente Auth, 2FAuth and other apps

- **Ente Auth:** Settings › Data › Export, and choose the plain-text option rather than *Encrypted*.
- **2FAuth:** select the accounts in *Manage* mode and choose Export: the JSON file works as it is.
- **Any other app:** an export that holds `otpauth://totp/…` links works, one link per line or separated by spaces.

An encrypted export of any of these is recognized, and the column asks you to export again without a password.

## Keeping the export safe

- **An export holds every seed in plain text.** Anyone with the file can make your codes. Once the column lists every account, delete it, empty the Trash, and delete it on your phone and from any cloud folder or chat it passed through. iCloud Drive and Photos keep deleted items in *Recently Deleted* for 30 days: empty that too, and remember that iCloud Photos copies a photo of a QR code to all your devices.
- **Copying it puts it on the clipboard, and so in yabbistir's history.** Delete that item right after you paste: select it in the panel and press ⌘⌫. The **Secret Guard** extension is a backstop: it keeps otpauth links and most authenticator exports out of the history, but only copies up to 256 KB. A larger one, such as an Aegis JSON export with icons, is saved like any other copy. Press ⌘⌫ either way.
- **In Settings, the export is kept in the Keychain** and never shown again: the field only says *Saved*.

### The trade-off

A second factor is worth most when it lives apart from your passwords: on a phone, while the passwords are on the Mac. Keeping the seeds on the same Mac as your passwords weakens that separation: someone who gets into your Mac while it is unlocked could get both. It trades some safety for convenience; make that trade knowingly, and keep your phone's authenticator as well.

## Limits

- **Time-based codes only (TOTP).** HOTP accounts are skipped: their counter has to be stored and moved forward on each use, and a pasted export cannot do that. Steam, mOTP and Yandex accounts are skipped too. When an export holds only accounts like these, the column says so.
- **SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512**, 6 to 10 digits, any period from 1 second to an hour (most accounts use SHA-1, 6 digits and 30 seconds).
- **Codes come from your Mac's clock.** If they are refused, check that the date and time are set automatically.
- **New accounts need a new export.** The column shows what is in Settings, nothing more.
- **Rows are sorted alphabetically** by service, then by account name.
- **Two accounts with the same names are both shown,** numbered in the export's order: *deniz · 1*, *deniz · 2*. This happens when an account was set up again and the old entry stayed. Remove the stale one in your authenticator app before you export.
- **Very large exports are untested** in the settings field and the Keychain. For a big vault, Aegis's text export is the smallest.

## Permissions and privacy

- **No permissions.** The extension does not reach the network, run programs, see your copies or read your history. It only reads its own *Accounts* setting.
- **Codes are never stored or shown.** A code is computed when you press ↵ and pasted, never written to yabbistir's history, the extension's storage, a file, a log or an error message. yabbistir pastes it as one item for this Mac only, marked so that clipboard managers (its own history included) skip it, and gives your clipboard back a moment later. When it cannot paste, without Accessibility access for example, it leaves the code on the clipboard for 30 seconds and says so.
- **Rows show only names.** A row has the service and the account name from your export; its id is the export's own id for the account, or a hash of those two names, never anything made from a seed.
- **The export is read, never kept.** yabbistir keeps it in the Keychain and hands it only to this extension, which reads it each time the panel opens or you press ↵ and keeps nothing from it between calls: no rows, no seeds, no codes.

Because it pastes secrets, the extension is marked sensitive. Before you install it, yabbistir tells you it "Can read and paste secrets such as passwords. They’re never written to history or disk."

# Jira

Your open Jira issues as a column in yabbistir's panel, and two actions for copied text: paste an issue key as a link, or turn a copied error into a new issue. Jira Cloud only, signed in with your email and an API token.

- **The *Jira* column** lists the issues assigned to you that are not done, the most recently updated first: up to 50, each as *ENG-42 Fix the login button*, with its status and project beneath. ↵ pastes the issue's link, ⇧↵ a Markdown link (`[ENG-42: Fix the login button](https://yourteam.atlassian.net/browse/ENG-42)`), and ⌘C copies the link.
- **Paste as Jira link**, on a copied issue key such as `ENG-42`, pastes `https://yourteam.atlassian.net/browse/ENG-42`. The row shows the link before you pick it.
- **Create Jira issue from this**, on copied text, makes a new issue in your project and pastes its link.

## Example

A teammate posts a stack trace in a chat. Copy it, open the panel, press ⇧ and pick *Create Jira issue from this*. Jira gets a new Task in your project:

- **Summary:** the first line with words in it, here `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')`.
- **Description:** the whole trace in a code block.

The new issue's link, such as `https://yourteam.atlassian.net/browse/ENG-101`, is pasted back into the chat.

Copied prose (a bug report, meeting notes) becomes paragraphs instead, with its line breaks kept. A single line that fits in the summary makes an issue with no description.

## Setup

1. Make an API token at [id.atlassian.com › Security › API tokens](https://id.atlassian.com/manage-profile/security/api-tokens). Choose **Create API token**, not *Create API token with scopes*: a scoped token works only through Atlassian's API gateway, which this extension does not reach. Tokens expire after 1 to 365 days; you pick when.
2. In yabbistir, open Settings → Extensions → Jira and fill in:
   - **Site:** your Jira Cloud address, such as `yourteam.atlassian.net`. `https://` and a link into the site, such as one copied from the browser, work too.
   - **Email:** the email you sign in to Jira with.
   - **API token:** the token from step 1. It is kept in the Keychain.
   - **Project key for new issues:** the key at the start of your project's issue keys, such as `ENG`. Jira now calls projects *spaces*; the key is the same.
   - **Issue type for new issues:** `Task` unless you change it, such as to `Bug`. It must be a type your project has, spelled as Jira shows it (Jira now calls these *work types*).

The column and the actions say what is missing until each part is set. Pasting an issue key as a link needs only the site.

## Permissions and privacy

- **network**, limited to `atlassian.net`. Every Jira Cloud site is `<name>.atlassian.net`, and the manifest cannot name your own, so the extension checks the Site setting itself: it must be exactly one name followed by `.atlassian.net`, without a user name or a port, and every request goes to that site over https, nowhere else. Redirects must stay inside `atlassian.net` too.
- **What is sent, and when.** Opening the panel searches your site for your open issues, at most once a minute. When Jira answers with an error, the column waits a minute before it asks again, or as long as Jira says when it limits requests. When Jira refuses your sign-in, the column does not send it again for 15 minutes, because several failed sign-ins in a row make Jira ask for a CAPTCHA; a changed site, email or token is tried at once. ⇧↵ on a row may ask your site for that issue's summary, when the column's list is more than five minutes old. *Create Jira issue from this* sends the copied text, as the new issue's summary and description, to your site when you pick it. *Paste as Jira link* sends nothing. Every request carries your email and API token, to your site only.
- **The token and the email are never written down or shown.** The token is read from the Keychain each time the column is listed, and when ⇧↵ or *Create Jira issue from this* sends a request. The email is kept in memory only, to tell one account's list from another's. Neither is written to the extension's storage, a file or a log, or put in a message. After Jira refuses a sign-in, the column keeps a short fingerprint of it in memory, which cannot be turned back into the email or the token, to know it when it comes again. Messages name your site, your project key and your issue type at most, never the copied text or Jira's own answers.
- **The column keeps nothing on disk.** Its list is reused for a minute and its summaries for five, in memory only; both are dropped when the column locks. yabbistir keeps the rows in memory until the Mac locks or sleeps, the column locks, or the app quits; they never reach yabbistir's history or the disk.

## When something goes wrong

- **Jira didn’t accept your email and API token:** check both in Settings. A token that has expired, or one made *with scopes*, is refused. Jira Cloud sometimes answers rejected credentials as if no one had asked, with an empty list; the extension reads Jira's sign-in header too, so such an answer locks the column instead of showing it empty.
- **Jira wants you to sign in on the web first:** after several failed sign-ins Jira asks for a CAPTCHA, and refuses API tokens until you sign in once in the browser. The column then tries again within 15 minutes, or at once when you change the site, email or token, or make an issue with *Create Jira issue from this*.
- **Jira is limiting requests:** the column waits as long as Jira asks (its `Retry-After`, at least a minute and at most a day) before asking again, and keeps the rows it has meanwhile.
- **Jira refused some fields for new issues:** your project requires a field this extension does not fill in (a component, a priority, a custom field), or does not take a description. Create that issue in Jira.
- **The text is too long for a Jira issue:** Jira found the description over its limit, although the extension cuts it to fit. Copy a shorter part, or create that issue in Jira.
- **A create that timed out or lost its connection** may still have made the issue in Jira. It is never sent twice by itself; look in Jira before you try again.

## Limits

- Jira Cloud only. Jira Data Center and Server sites are not on `atlassian.net`, and sign in differently.
- One page of the search: the 50 most recently updated issues. Jira's search may take a moment to show an issue you just changed.
- A summary is cut at 254 characters (Jira takes fewer than 255). A description is cut so that its document stays within 30,000 characters, under the 32,767 Jira takes. Jira counts the whole document, not the text alone: each line of prose adds a few dozen characters, and each quote or line end in a code block one more, so many short lines hold less text. When a description is cut, its end shows `…` and a notice says how many characters it holds.
- Whether copied text is code or a log is a guess from its lines: stack frames from JavaScript, Java, Python, Go, Rust, gdb, lldb and macOS crash reports, timestamped or leveled log lines, JSON, and lines that read as code. Indented lines count only beside lines that read as code, so a note with an indented or nested list stays prose. Copies yabbistir already marks as code always go into a code block.
- Terminal color codes and other control characters are left out of a new issue.
- The issue key action is offered on keys alone (`ENG-42`), not on keys inside a sentence or on links. It is also offered on look-alikes such as `UTF-8` or `SHA-256`; the row's hint shows the link it would paste.

## Sources

- Search: [Search for issues using JQL enhanced search](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/rest/v3/api-group-issue-search/#api-rest-api-3-search-jql-get) (`GET /rest/api/3/search/jql`), which replaced the removed `/rest/api/3/search` ([CHANGE-2046](https://developer.atlassian.com/changelog/#CHANGE-2046)). It returns only issue ids unless `fields` names more.
- Create: [Create issue](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/rest/v3/api-group-issues/#api-rest-api-3-issue-post) (`POST /rest/api/3/issue`), and the [Atlassian Document Format](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/apis/document/structure/) for the description. A description over 32,767 characters is refused with `CONTENT_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` ([JRACLOUD-78553](https://jira.atlassian.com/browse/JRACLOUD-78553)), counted on the whole document ([JRACLOUD-98152](https://jira.atlassian.com/browse/JRACLOUD-98152)).
- Sign-in: [Basic auth for REST APIs](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/basic-auth-for-rest-apis/) and [Manage API tokens](https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-account/docs/manage-api-tokens-for-your-atlassian-account/); rejected credentials answered with a 200: [JRACLOUD-82932](https://jira.atlassian.com/browse/JRACLOUD-82932).
- Limits: [Rate limiting](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/rate-limiting/).

The extension embeds no data from these pages.

# Bitwarden

Your Bitwarden logins in yabbistir's panel, through [bw](https://bitwarden.com/help/cli/), Bitwarden's official command-line tool. It adds two columns:

- **Bitwarden**: every login, with its name, and its username and site below. ↵ pastes the password, ⇧↵ pastes the username, and ⌘C copies the username.
- **Bitwarden codes**: the logins that have an authenticator key. ↵ pastes the current TOTP code.

A column has room for two actions, ↵ and ⇧↵, so the codes get a column of their own. Favorites come first, then the rest by name. Secure notes, cards, identities and SSH keys are left out.

## Example

Click into a login form's password field, open the panel and move to the *Bitwarden* column. Type `posta` to find *Posta* (`deniz.k · posta.ornek.dev`) and press ↵: the password is pasted, and your clipboard comes back a moment later. When the site then asks for a code, open the panel again, move to *Bitwarden codes* and press ↵ on *Posta*.

The site in a row is the host of the login's first web address, and it is left out when the login is named after it: *ornek.dev* shows only `deniz.k`.

## Setup

Install bw, then log in once in Terminal:

```sh
brew install bitwarden-cli
bw login --raw
```

bw asks for your email, your master password and, if your account has one, a second factor, then prints a **session key**. Copy it, open Settings → Extensions → Bitwarden and paste it into *Session key*. The extension never asks for your master password.

- Already logged in? Run `bw unlock --raw` instead; it prints a new key.
- You can also paste the whole `export BW_SESSION="…"` line that `bw unlock` prints without `--raw`.
- Logged in with an API key (`bw login --apikey`) or through single sign-on (`bw login --sso`)? That does not unlock the vault: run `bw unlock --raw` after it.
- A self-hosted server, or Bitwarden's EU cloud, is set in bw itself, before you log in: `bw config server https://vault.example.com` (or `https://vault.bitwarden.eu`). The extension uses whatever server bw uses.
- yabbistir runs bw with a small environment of its own (`PATH`, `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `USER` and `LANG`), not your shell's. So bw must keep its data in its usual place: if you moved it with `BITWARDENCLI_APPDATA_DIR`, the column says to log in even though bw in Terminal is logged in.

Until a key is in Settings, the column shows one row that says what to do. Press ↵ or ⌘C on it to copy the command (`bw login --raw` or `bw unlock --raw`), and run it in Terminal.

## How long the session key lasts

The key does not expire. It keeps working after the Mac sleeps, locks or restarts, until you run `bw lock` or `bw logout`, or run `bw unlock` again, since every new key ends the ones before it. Unlike the Bitwarden app, the column has no vault timeout: run `bw lock` when you step away, and paste a new key when you come back.

Once the key has ended, the column says *Bitwarden is locked* and the rows go. Press ↵ or ⌘C on that row to copy `bw unlock --raw`, run it, and paste the new key in Settings. So if you also use bw in Terminal, unlocking it there ends the key in yabbistir too.

## New items

bw keeps a local copy of your vault and does not fetch changes on its own, and the extension never syncs. An item you add or change elsewhere shows up after bw syncs: run `bw sync` in Terminal. The column also reuses its list for up to five minutes.

## Master password re-prompt

Items you protect with Bitwarden's *Master password re-prompt* are listed in the *Bitwarden* column, and their username pastes, but their password never does, and they are left out of *Bitwarden codes*: yabbistir cannot ask for your master password, and pasting without it would skip the check you turned on. ↵ on such an item says *This item asks for your master password first* instead. Turn re-prompt off for an item to paste it from yabbistir.

## TOTP codes

bw makes TOTP codes for Bitwarden Premium accounts, and for organization items whose organization includes them; otherwise the column says *TOTP codes need Bitwarden Premium.* A code is made when you press ↵ and is valid until its window ends, usually within 30 seconds.

## Limits

- **Logins only.** Notes, cards, identities and SSH keys are not listed. A login that holds a passkey is listed, but the passkey itself cannot be pasted, and a login with only a passkey has no password to paste.
- **Hidden passwords.** An organization can let you use an item without seeing its password. bw gives the extension neither that password nor its code, so it says there is none to paste.
- **Speed.** bw takes a second or more to start. Each time the panel opens, `bw status` runs once, shared by both columns, to check the lock; when the list is older than five minutes, `bw list items` runs instead. A TOTP code takes two bw runs, one after the other: the item first, to check for a re-prompt, then the code. A bw that takes longer than nine seconds is stopped, and the extension says so.
- **A very large vault, or a slow Mac, may not list within nine seconds.**

## Permissions and privacy

- **exec**, limited to `bw`. The extension runs `bw status`, `bw list items`, `bw get item`, `bw get username` and `bw get totp`, always with `--nointeraction --response` (never ask, answer in JSON), and with `--session` and your key, except for one `bw status` without a key, which tells whether to log in or to unlock. The only other argument is an item's id, which must be a Bitwarden id before it reaches bw: bw would treat anything else as a search, which could find another item. It never runs `bw sync`, never uses bw's clipboard, never changes bw's server, and asks for no network permission.
- **bw can read your whole vault** once it has the key. `bw list items` prints every item in full, passwords included. The extension reads that output in memory and keeps, for each login, only its id, name, username, the host of its first web address (never the rest of the address), whether it is a favorite, whether it has an authenticator key and whether it asks for a re-prompt; everything else is dropped at once. For ↵ in either column it runs `bw get item`, which tells whether the item asks for a re-prompt right now.
- **The session key** is kept by yabbistir in your Keychain, and only bw gets it. Only text shaped like a key bw makes reaches bw: a master password typed there by mistake never does. yabbistir cannot hand a program an environment variable, so the key goes on bw's command line with its own `--session` option. Each time the panel opens, and each time you paste from a Bitwarden column, the key is on that command line for as long as bw runs (a second or more; longer for a large vault). Programs running as you can read it then, and security software that records program launches may keep it in its logs. With the key and bw's data, the vault can be read until the key ends: run `bw lock` to end it at any time. The key never appears in a row, a message or a log.
- **Passwords and codes are never stored or shown.** Not in yabbistir's history, not in the extension's storage or a file, not in a log and not in an error message. yabbistir pastes them as one item for this Mac only, marked so that clipboard managers (its own history included) skip it, and gives your clipboard back a moment later. When it cannot paste, without Accessibility access for example, it leaves the value on the clipboard for 30 seconds and says so.
- **An empty password is never pasted.** When an item has none, the extension says so instead.
- **The list stays in memory only.** The extension reuses its list for up to five minutes, keeps with it a short fingerprint of the key that read it (never the key), and forgets it when bw locks. yabbistir keeps the rows in memory until the Mac locks or sleeps, Bitwarden locks, or the app quits. They never reach yabbistir's history, its search index or the disk.

Because it can paste secrets, the extension is marked sensitive. Before you install it, yabbistir tells you it "Can read and paste secrets such as passwords. They’re never written to history or disk."

# Hash & Encode

Hashes and encodings for text and code, everything computed on this Mac. Pick an item, press ⇧, and the transform is there; decoders show up only when the text can be decoded, and every decoder shows its result on the row before you paste. Hash rows show no preview.

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Hash** (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512) | The digest of the text's UTF-8 bytes, as lowercase hex |
| **Encode for a URL** / **Decode from a URL** | Percent-encoding of a component (`encodeURIComponent`) and back; decoding is offered when the text has `%XX` |
| **Encode HTML entities** / **Decode HTML entities** | `& < > " '` and every non-ASCII character as `&#N;`, and back (named and numeric references) |
| **Escape as Unicode** / **Unescape Unicode** | Non-ASCII characters as `\uXXXX` (an emoji as its surrogate pair), and `\uXXXX`, `\u{XXXXX}`, `\xXX` back |
| **Text to hex** / **Hex to text** | UTF-8 bytes as hex, and back; decoding is offered for pairs of hex digits |
| **ROT13** | Rotates the letters A to Z by 13; offered when there is a letter |
| **Domain to Punycode** / **Punycode to domain** | `bücher.example` to `xn--bcher-kva.example` (RFC 3492), on a domain or a link |

## Example

Copy `Şişli`, press ⇧, choose **Escape as Unicode**: `Şişli`. Copy `caf%C3%A9`, choose **Decode from a URL**: `café`. Copy `https://bücher.example/yol`, choose **Domain to Punycode**: `https://xn--bcher-kva.example/yol`.

## Details and limits

- **Hash** covers the text exactly as copied: a trailing newline changes the digest. Text is hashed as UTF-8. MD5 and SHA-1 are here for checksums and compatibility, not for security. Hashes are written in plain TypeScript (the extension host has no hashing of its own) and checked against the official test vectors and against Node's `crypto`.
- **URL**: decoding handles each run of `%XX` that is valid UTF-8; a stray `%` or a byte that is not text stays as written. `+` is not turned into a space (that is form decoding). Encoding leaves `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ . ! ~ * ' ( )` as they are, like `encodeURIComponent`. A link is decoded from its address.
- **HTML**: decoding knows the common named set (Latin-1, Greek, arrows, math symbols, typographic punctuation, `'`), decimal and hexadecimal references, and treats numbers 128 to 159 as Windows-1252, as HTML does. Names it does not know, and references without the closing `;`, are left as written. It decodes once: `&lt;` becomes `<`.
- **Unicode escapes**: only characters past ASCII are escaped. Decoding leaves malformed escapes, lone surrogates and code points past U+10FFFF as written, and does not decode an escaped backslash (`\\u0041`).
- **Hex**: decoding accepts spaces, line breaks, colons and a leading `0x` between and before pairs, and refuses bytes that are not valid UTF-8 with a message.
- **Punycode**: only the host of a link is converted; a path, query or fragment with non-ASCII characters is left alone. Labels are lowercased and normalized (NFC) before encoding; this is not the full UTS #46 mapping. A label longer than 63 characters is refused.
- Hex decoding also refuses results that contain control characters (other than tab and line breaks), so a digit string like `0102` is not read as text.
- Previews on very large text (several hundred KB) may be skipped when they would take too long; the action itself still works.
- Punycode is offered only on domain-like text: no spaces, at least one dot and a non-ASCII character.
- All of it is linear in the text's size; a megabyte is far inside the 10-second limit.

## Permissions and tools

None. No network, no programs, no history: everything is computed from the item you picked.

## Sources

- Hash algorithms: RFC 1321 (MD5) and FIPS 180-4 (SHA-1, SHA-2); the SHA-2 constants are derived at load time from the square and cube roots of the first primes, as that standard defines them.
- Punycode: RFC 3492, with its section 7.1 sample strings as tests.
- HTML entity names: the mapping of names to characters from the [HTML Living Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/named-characters.html) (WHATWG; names and code points are facts, no text is copied). The extension carries its common subset only.
readmes.dev.yabbistir.docker:
# Docker

Your Docker containers as a column in yabbistir's panel, through the `docker` command-line tool. Each row shows a container's name, and under it the image, the status and the published ports. ↵ pastes the name, ⇧↵ pastes `docker exec -it <name> sh`, and ⌘C copies the name.

It works with Docker Desktop, OrbStack and Colima, since each of them provides the `docker` command.

## Example

You are in a terminal and want a shell in your database. Open the panel, move to the *Containers* column, type `db` to find *ornek-db* (`postgres:16 · Up 2 hours · 5432→5432/tcp`) and press ⇧↵: `docker exec -it ornek-db sh` is pasted, ready to run. Press ↵ instead to paste just the name, for `docker logs -f` or any other command.

## Settings

- **Include stopped containers**: off by default, so the column lists running containers only. Turn it on to list stopped ones too (`docker ps --all`); their status says, for example, *Exited (0) 3 days ago*.

## Permissions and tools

- **`exec`**, to run `docker ps`. That is the only command the extension runs; it never starts, stops, removes or enters a container. The commands it pastes are for you to run.
- **`docker`**: `brew install --cask docker` installs Docker Desktop; OrbStack (`brew install --cask orbstack`) and Colima (`brew install colima docker`) provide the command too.

There is no network permission, and nothing is written to disk. The extension keeps no rows between listings.

## When Docker is not running

The column shows *Docker isn’t running* when `docker` cannot reach its engine (the app is closed, or Colima is stopped). Start it and open the panel again. The messages `docker` prints when it cannot reach the engine (*Cannot connect to the Docker daemon*, *error during connect*, a missing `docker.sock`) are what the extension recognizes; any other failure is reported as a plain error without docker's text. When the engine answers *permission denied* (your user may not use the socket, for example outside the `docker` group), the column says *Docker refused access* instead. If `docker` itself is missing, yabbistir tells you which tool to install.

## Limits

- Listing has a time limit of 10 seconds. While Docker Desktop is still starting, `docker ps` can take longer, and the list is cancelled without a row; open the panel again once Docker is up.
- A container name is limited to 128 characters; a longer one is not listed.
- The pasted exec command opens `sh`. A container without `sh` (a distroless image) needs another command.
- A container's name is its row's identity, so renaming a container shows it as a new row.
- Link aliases (`webapp/db`) are not shown; the container's own name is.
- Ports are shown without the host address, and the IPv4 and IPv6 twins are merged: `0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp, :::8080->80/tcp` reads `8080→80/tcp`. After three ports, the rest is counted (`+2`).
- Docker's `--format '{{json .}}'` output is documented at <https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/ls/>.

## Develop

```sh
npm test -- dev.yabbistir.docker
npm run build -- dev.yabbistir.docker
```

# Color Tools

Tells you what a copied color is close to, whether text is readable on it, and gives you lighter, darker and opposite versions. It adds what the built-in Convert does not: Convert changes a color's format (RGB, HSL, OKLCH, SwiftUI, NSColor); Color Tools works with the color itself.

## What it does

**Preview.** Every color item is tagged *color*, and its preview shows:

- **Nearest:** the closest CSS named color and the closest Tailwind CSS color (`slate-500` style), each with its distance, or *exact* when it is the same color. The distance is ΔE in OKLab, times 100: below 1 is hard to tell apart, around 2 to 3 is a small difference.
- **Contrast:** the WCAG 2.x contrast ratio on white and on black, with the level reached for normal text and for large text (AA needs 4.5:1 and 3:1, AAA needs 7:1 and 4.5:1), and the relative luminance.

**Actions** on a color, each returning text you can paste (a hint shows the value on the row):

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Make 10, 20 or 30% lighter | Hex, moved toward white |
| Make 10, 20 or 30% darker | Hex, moved toward black |
| Complementary color | Hex, hue turned half a circle |
| Invert color | Hex, every channel flipped |
| Make gray | Hex, same lightness with no hue |
| Paste as Tailwind name | The nearest Tailwind name, such as `slate-500` |

## Example

Copy `#777777` from a design tool. The preview says: nearest CSS name *gray* (ΔE 3.1), nearest Tailwind *neutral-500* (ΔE 1.4); on white `4.48:1`, *Normal text fails · Large text AA*. *Make 20% darker* pastes `#575757`; *Paste as Tailwind name* pastes `neutral-500`.

## How the numbers are made

- **Lighter and darker** mix in OKLab: the lightness moves the given share of the way to white or black and the color's chroma shrinks by the same share. Steps look even and the hue stays put.
- **Complementary** turns the hue by 180 degrees in HSL, keeping saturation and lightness (the usual color wheel).
- **Gray** keeps OKLab lightness, so a red and a blue of equal brightness give the same gray.
- **Contrast** follows WCAG 2.x: luminance from linear sRGB with the 0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722 weights, ratio `(L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05)`. It is shown to two decimals but never rounded up across a pass mark, so `4.499` is not shown as `4.50`.
- **Nearest** is the smallest OKLab distance. The first palette entry wins a tie, and Tailwind lists `zinc-50` before `neutral-50`.
- **Alpha.** A color with transparency is compared as it looks on white: names, distances and contrast all use the color composited on white, and the preview says so. The actions keep the original alpha and write it into the result (`#rrggbbaa`) when it is below 100%; *Paste as Tailwind name* is based on the composited color.

## Permissions

None. The extension only reads the color of the item it is asked about and computes on this Mac. No network, no programs, nothing stored.

## Limits

- Only the Tailwind CSS v3 default palette is known, not custom or v4 colors.
- Results are hex text. The format is up to you; use the built-in Convert for other formats.
- The CSS names are the 141 distinct names of CSS Color Module Level 4 (the `grey` spellings are left out, `gray` is kept).
- Lighter, darker and complementary colors are clipped into the sRGB range, so very saturated colors can shift a little.

## Data and licenses

- CSS named colors: values from the [color-name](https://github.com/colorjs/color-name) package 1.1.4, MIT license, copyright (c) 2015 Dmitry Ivanov.
- Tailwind CSS v3 default colors: from [tailwindcss](https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss) 3.4.17 (`src/public/colors.js`), MIT license, copyright (c) Tailwind Labs, Inc. Tailwind CSS is a trademark of Tailwind Labs; this extension is not affiliated with it.
- OKLab: Björn Ottosson, "A perceptual color space for image processing" (2020), public domain. WCAG: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.x, relative luminance and contrast ratio definitions.

# Calculator

Copy a sum from a spreadsheet, an invoice or a chat, and yabbistir tags it and pastes the answer.

## Example

Copy `12 * 3 + 4`: the item gets the *calc* tag, its preview shows *Result: 40* and *Expression: 12 * 3 + 4*, and two actions are offered with the answer on the row:

- **Paste result** pastes `40`.
- **Paste expression = result** pastes `12 * 3 + 4 = 40`.

More that works: `15% of 80` (12), `80 + 15%` (92), `80 * 15%` (12), `(2 + 3) × 4`, `2^3^2` (512), `1.234,56 + 10` (1.244,56), `sqrt(16) + 1`, `max(1, 7) - min(4; 2)`.

## What it understands

- Numbers, `+ - * / × ÷ ^`, `%` as percent or remainder, parentheses, unary minus. `^` is right to left and binds tighter than unary minus: `2^3^2` is 512, `-2^2` is -4.
- Percentages: `15% of 80`, `80 + 15%` (80 plus 15% of 80), `80 - 15%`, `80 * 15%`. `10 % 3` (a space and an operand after it) is the remainder, 1.
- Functions: `sqrt abs round floor ceil sin cos tan log ln exp min max`. `log` is base 10, `ln` is natural, trigonometry is in radians, `round(x; digits)` takes an optional second argument. Separate arguments with `;` or with a comma followed by a space (`max(1, 2)`); a comma with no space after it is a decimal comma.
- Constants `pi` (or `π`) and `e`.
- A trailing or leading `=` is ignored.

## Number styles

Dot or comma decimals and thousands marks both work: `1.234,56` and `1,234.56`. When a number is clear (`1.234,56`, `1,5`, `1.5`, `1.234.567`) it is read as written. A single separator followed by exactly three digits (`1.234`, `1,234`) is ambiguous, and the app's language decides: in English the comma is the thousands mark, in Turkish (and German, French and so on) the dot is. The answer is written in the style of the input: the same decimal mark, and with thousands marks when the input had them. The answer has at most 12 significant digits; very large or tiny answers use an exponent (`1.26765060023e30`).

## What is not tagged

Anything that fails to parse: division by zero, overflow, unknown words, `sqrt(-1)`. A lone number, a lone percentage or a lone constant (no operator), text over 5,000 characters, and text on several lines. Things that look like a sum but are not: dates (`2024-11-04`, `11/04/2024`, `2024-11`), phone numbers (`555-123-4567`, `555-1234`), version strings (`1.2.3`), IP addresses, zero-padded numbers (`007`), times, `1920x1080`.

## Permissions

None. The extension reads only the item it is asked about. No network, no programs, no history.

## How it works

A tokenizer and a recursive-descent parser that evaluates as it reads: no `eval`, no `Function`. Parsing is linear in the text and nesting is limited, so a very long or adversarial copy is rejected quickly (the detector has 50 ms).

## Limits

- Write a subtraction of two plain numbers of three or more digits with spaces (`555 - 1234`): without spaces it is taken for a phone number or an identifier. Chains like `10-5-2` without spaces are taken for dates for the same reason; with spaces they are sums.
- Short joined pairs such as `2-1` or `10-12` (scores, page ranges, hours) and `e-1` are not tagged; add spaces (`2 - 1`) to get a sum.
- A comma without a space is a decimal comma, so in an English app `max(1,7)` is not tagged; write `max(1; 7)` or `max(1, 7)`. In Turkish `max(1,7)` is read as the single number 1,7.
- A bare function call such as `sqrt(16)` is tagged even without an operator; a remainder followed by a percent (`5 % 2%`) is not tagged.
- No implicit multiplication (`2(3)`, `2pi`), no `x` as times, no units or currencies, no scientific notation input (`1e3`).
- Numbers with spaces or apostrophes as thousands marks (`1 234`, `1'234`) are not read.
- Floating point: results are rounded to 12 digits, so tiny differences (`0.1 + 0.2`) vanish.

# Change Case

Changes the case of copied text or code, and shows the result on the row before you paste it. One action, **Change case**, with eleven variants:

| Variant | `HTTPServerError` / `the lord of the rings` becomes |
|---|---|
| camelCase | `httpServerError` |
| PascalCase | `HttpServerError` |
| snake_case | `http_server_error` |
| CONSTANT_CASE | `HTTP_SERVER_ERROR` |
| kebab-case | `http-server-error` |
| dot.case | `http.server.error` |
| Title Case | `The Lord of the Rings` |
| Sentence case | `The lord of the rings` |
| UPPERCASE / lowercase | `THE LORD OF THE RINGS` / `the lord of the rings` |
| URL slug | `the-lord-of-the-rings` |

## Example

Copy `parseHTTPResponse2Json`, open the actions, type `snake`: the row shows `parse_http_response2_json`. ↵ pastes it.

## How words are found

- camelCase and PascalCase boundaries, and acronyms: `HTTPServerError` is *http, server, error*.
- Separators: spaces, `_`, `-`, `.` and any punctuation. An apostrophe inside a word is dropped (`don't` is `dont`).
- Digits stay with the letters beside them (`base64Encode` is *base64, encode*), and split only before a capital (`v2Beta` is *v2, beta*).
- Emoji and CJK text are treated as part of a word and passed through unchanged.

Title Case and Sentence case keep your punctuation and spacing. They split camelCase and `_ - .` only when the whole line is one token (`helloWorld` becomes `Hello World`); a single leading lower-case letter stays with its word (`iPhone` becomes `Iphone`, not `I Phone`); in a sentence, a word like `iPhone` is only lower-cased and capitalized as a whole.

## Casing rules (Turkish)

The *Casing rules* setting is **Automatic** (the app's language), **Turkish** or **English**. Turkish rules map `i` to `İ` and `ı` to `I` (`istanbul` becomes `İSTANBUL`, `IŞIK` becomes `ışık`); English rules do not (`ISTANBUL`). Title Case keeps these words small in the middle of a title: English *a, an, and, as, at, but, by, for, in, nor, of, on, or, the, to, via, vs*; Turkish *ve, ile, veya*. The rules apply to UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title Case, Sentence case and the slug. The code variants (camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, CONSTANT_CASE, kebab-case, dot.case) always use English rules so identifiers stay plain ASCII-safe (`getUserID` becomes `get_user_id`, never `get_user_ıd`).

## Slug

Lower-cases (with the chosen rules), transliterates Turkish letters and other accents (`ç ğ ı İ ö ş ü`, `é`, `ß`, `æ`, `ø`, `ł`…) and keeps only `a-z` and `0-9`, joined by single hyphens. Text with nothing URL-safe in it (only CJK or emoji) pastes nothing and says so.

## Lines

Multi-line text is converted line by line: line breaks, blank lines, and each line's leading and trailing whitespace stay as they are. In Sentence and Title case every line starts with a capital.

## Permissions and tools

None. The extension only reads the item it is given and returns text; it uses no network, runs no programs and keeps nothing.

## Limits

- Empty or whitespace-only text pastes nothing and says so.
- Sentence case treats a stop after a single letter as an abbreviation (`e.g. this`) and does not capitalize after it; other abbreviations (`Dr. smith`) do start a new sentence.
- English "I" is fixed in Sentence case (`i think` becomes `I think`) only under English rules.
- Long text is fine: work grows linearly and 60,000 characters take a few milliseconds, well within the hint's 500 ms.

## Develop

```sh
npm test -- dev.yabbistir.change-case
npm run build -- dev.yabbistir.change-case
```

# HTML to Markdown Adds **Paste as Markdown** to text you copy with its formatting, from a web page, Google Docs, Notion, Word or Outlook. The row shows the Markdown before you pick it, and that Markdown is what gets pasted: headings, lists, links, tables and code come out as clean Markdown for your notes, READMEs and docs. ## Example Copy this from a web page: > **Release notes** > > - Faster search, see [the guide](https://example.com/guide) > - Fixed a crash in `sync` Press ⇧ on the item and choose *Paste as Markdown*: ```markdown **Release notes** - Faster search, see [the guide](https://example.com/guide) - Fixed a crash in `sync` ``` ## What it converts - Headings, paragraphs and line breaks. - Bold, italic, strikethrough and inline code, from tags and from the inline styles editors use (`font-weight: 700`, `font-style: italic`, `text-decoration: line-through`). - Links with their titles, and images with their description, address and title. A link whose text is its own address becomes ``. - Bulleted, numbered and nested lists, with each list's starting number, and task lists (`- [x]`). - Block quotes, horizontal rules and code blocks, with the language when the page names it (`language-js`, `lang-js`, `highlight-source-js`, `data-lang`). - Tables, with the column alignment the page sets. Cells that span columns or rows leave the cells they cover empty. - Entities such as `&` and `’`, and white space the way a browser shows it. - Characters Markdown could read as syntax get a backslash: `*`, `` ` ``, `[` and `]` always, and the start of a line that would read as a heading, a list item, a quote or a table rule (`#`, `-`, `1.`, `>`, `-- | --`). An underscore inside a word, as in `snake_case`, stays as it is. It knows the quirks of the apps you copy from: - **Google Docs**: the whole copy is wrapped in bold that isn't bold, nested lists sit beside their parent item, and checklists keep their ticks. - **Notion**: to-do lists keep their state, and lists split into one item each are joined again. - **Word and Outlook**: bullets and numbers written as paragraphs become real nested lists, and the stylesheet, conditional comments, `` and hidden text are left out. - **Safari and Chrome**: bold and italic written as inline styles count, and the styles a browser adds to everything do not. - **Code editors**: code copied as colored lines in a monospaced font becomes a code block. ## Limits - It needs the copy's formatting. Plain text, and copies whose formatting is larger than 256 KB (yabbistir doesn't pass those to extensions), get the message *This copy has no formatting to turn into Markdown*. - Relative links stay as they are, since the page they came from isn't known. - Images stored inside the copy, rather than at an address, are left out; their description stays as text. Images copied from Word point to temporary files on your Mac. - Underline, highlight, colors, font sizes, and superscript and subscript have no Markdown, so that text stays plain. - A table cell is one line: its paragraphs and line breaks become `
`. A table used for layout, such as an email's columns or a cell holding a list or heading, is read as its content instead. - In Google Docs and Word, text in a monospaced font such as Courier is code: a paragraph of it becomes a code block, a few words become inline code. When the whole copy is in that font, it stays text. On web pages, only real code elements count. - Markdown cannot show a few combinations, such as bold that ends in punctuation right before a letter (`**Note:**then`); those may lose their bold. ## Permissions None. The extension reads only the item you pick, and converts it on your Mac. ## Data The names of HTML's character entities come from the [WHATWG HTML Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/named-characters.html), used under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

# GitHub

The pull requests and issues that wait on you, as a column in yabbistir's panel, and a way to share copied code as a gist. It works through [`gh`](https://cli.github.com), GitHub's official command-line tool, with your own `gh` login.

## The column

Each row is one open item, with a subtitle that says which group it is in and where it lives:

- `Review requested · owner/repo #123`: pull requests waiting for your review (review requested from you directly, not through a team).
- `Your pull request · owner/repo #124` (or `Your draft pull request`): your open pull requests.
- `Assigned to you · owner/repo #125`: open issues assigned to you.

The groups come in that order, each with its most recently updated item first and at most 25 items. Search filters by title and by the subtitle, so typing a repository name or `review` narrows the list.

- ↵ pastes the link: `https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123`
- ⇧↵ pastes a Markdown link: `[owner/repo#123: Title](https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123)`
- ⌘C copies the link.

A row can have two actions, so the short reference `owner/repo#123` is not on the row. It is an action on a link instead: copy a GitHub pull request or issue link (from the address bar, say), open the panel on it and choose *Paste short reference*.

## Share as gist

Choose *Share as gist* on copied text or code and pick *Share as secret gist* (the default: only people with the link can see it) or *Share as public gist* (listed on your GitHub profile). The extension writes the text into a file in its work folder, named `clipboard.txt` or, for code it recognizes (JSON, shell, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Swift, HTML, XML), `clipboard.json`, `clipboard.py` and so on, runs `gh gist create`, and returns the gist's link. ↵ pastes it, ⌘C copies it. The gist has no description, so nothing about yabbistir is published with it.

## Setup

```sh
brew install gh
gh auth login
```

Signing in always happens in Terminal. Sign in with `gh auth login`: yabbistir starts `gh` with a minimal environment, so a login that exists only as a `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` variable in your shell is not seen, and the column says you are not signed in. When you are not signed in, the column shows *Not signed in to GitHub*; press ↵ or ⌘C on that row to copy `gh auth login`, and run it in Terminal.

## Permissions and privacy

- **exec**, limited to `gh`. The extension runs `gh search prs`, `gh search issues` and `gh gist create`, always with fixed options. The only other argument is the path of the file it just wrote in its work folder.
- **No network permission.** `gh` talks to GitHub with your own `gh` login; the extension never sees or stores a token, and it cannot reach the network itself.
- **What GitHub is asked.** Opening the panel searches GitHub for open items that name you (`@me`) as reviewer, author or assignee. Rows stay in memory for a minute, then are listed again, and are never written to disk. For that minute the last list is served without asking `gh`, even after `gh auth logout`; the column locks at the next listing. GitHub allows 30 searches a minute, three per listing.
- **A gist leaves your Mac** only when you choose the action, with exactly the text of the item you chose it on. A secret gist is not listed anywhere, but anyone with its link can read it.
- Nothing from `gh`'s output, errors included, is written to a log or shown in a message.

## Limits

- github.com only. GitHub Enterprise hosts are not listed.
- Team review requests are not included; only reviews requested from you. GitHub drops a pull request from "review requested" once you have posted a review, until you are requested again, so it can seem to go missing.
- If one or two of the three searches fail (a rate limit, say), the groups that worked are shown and the next opening asks again.
- In a Markdown link, `\ [ ] < > & * _` in the title are escaped so the link pastes as written; backticks are kept, so a `code` span in a title stays one.
- Written against `gh` 2.67; it needs `gh search` with `--json`, so keep `gh` up to date (`brew upgrade gh`).

# JWT

Recognizes copied JSON Web Tokens and shows what is inside: the header, the payload and a short summary (algorithm, type, subject, issued and expiry time). An expired token is marked as such.

The token is decoded on this Mac and nothing more. **The signature is not checked**, and the preview says so. Text that is not a well-formed token (wrong shape, bad encoding, no `alg` in the header, a payload that is not an object, or longer than 16 KB) is not tagged.

## Permissions

None. The extension reads only the item it is asked about.

# LastPass

Your LastPass entries as a column in yabbistir's panel, through [lpass](https://github.com/lastpass/lastpass-cli), LastPass's command-line tool. Each row shows a site's name and its username; folders and secure notes are left out. ↵ pastes the password, ⇧↵ pastes the username, and ⌘C copies the username.

## Example

Click into a login form's password field, open the panel and move to the *LastPass* column. Type `ornek` to find *ornek.dev* (`deniz.k`) and press ↵: the password is pasted, and your clipboard comes back a moment later.

## Setup

Install lpass, then log in once in Terminal:

```sh
brew install lastpass-cli
lpass login --trust <email>
```

Logging in always happens in Terminal: lpass asks for your master password there, and for a second factor if your account has one. The extension never asks for either.

lpass 1.6.2 or later is needed, since older versions can no longer connect to LastPass. When the column says *lpass needs an update*, press ↵ or ⌘C on that row to copy `brew upgrade lastpass-cli`, and run it in Terminal.

## Staying unlocked

After you log in, lpass keeps your vault unlocked in a background agent for a while. When the agent stops, the column shows *LastPass is locked* with the login command: press ↵ or ⌘C to copy it, and run it in Terminal.

To stay unlocked longer, set the agent's timeout, in seconds, in `~/.lpass/env`. For eight hours, add this line:

```sh
LPASS_AGENT_TIMEOUT=28800
```

## New entries

The extension runs lpass with `--sync=no`: it lists and reads lpass's local copy of your vault and does not sync on the way, which keeps the panel quick. The one exception is right after you log in again: `lpass logout` deletes that copy and `lpass login` does not fetch it, so when the local copy is missing the extension asks lpass to fetch it once. An entry you add or change elsewhere shows up after lpass syncs; run `lpass sync` in Terminal to get it now. The column also reuses its list for up to five minutes.

## Not supported

Accounts that log in with a FIDO2 security key, or through single sign-on (SSO): lpass cannot log in to them, so this extension cannot list them.

## Permissions and privacy

- **exec**, limited to `lpass`. The extension runs `lpass --version`, `lpass status -q`, `lpass ls` and `lpass show`, always with fixed options. The only other argument is an entry's id, which must be a number before it reaches lpass. It never uses lpass's own clipboard option, and it asks for no network permission.
- **lpass can read your whole vault** once you are logged in. For the list, the extension reads each entry's name, username and URL; the URL only to leave out folders and secure notes, and it is never kept or shown. It reads one entry's password or username when you press ↵, ⇧↵ or ⌘C on its row.
- **Passwords are never stored or shown.** Not in yabbistir's history, not in the extension's storage or a file, not in a log and not in an error message. yabbistir pastes a password as one item for this Mac only, marked so that clipboard managers (its own history included) skip it, and gives your clipboard back a moment later. When it cannot paste, without Accessibility access for example, it leaves the password on the clipboard for 30 seconds and says so.
- **An empty password is never pasted.** When lpass cannot decrypt an entry, it prints an empty field; the extension says so instead.
- **The list stays in memory only.** The extension reuses its list for up to five minutes, and yabbistir keeps the rows in memory until the Mac locks or sleeps, LastPass locks, or the app quits. They never reach yabbistir's history, its search index or the disk.

Because it can paste secrets, the extension is marked sensitive. Before you install it, yabbistir tells you it "Can read and paste secrets such as passwords. They’re never written to history or disk."
readmes.dev.yabbistir.link-clean:
# Link Cleaner

Strips tracking parameters from the links you copy, as they are captured. A link such as `https://example.com/p?id=7&utm_source=mail&fbclid=1` is stored as `https://example.com/p?id=7`.

- Removes `utm_*` and well-known click and campaign identifiers on every site.
- Removes a few share tokens on the sites that add them (for example `si` and `feature` on video links).
- Keeps every other parameter, the fragment and the rest of the address. A link with nothing to remove is left alone.
- Works on a copied link, or on text that is one address and nothing else. Other text never reaches the extension.

## Permissions

- **capture**: to rewrite an item before it enters your history. The extension does not read the clipboard at any other time and has no network access.
readmes.dev.yabbistir.homebrew:
# Homebrew

[Homebrew](https://brew.sh), the Mac's package manager, from yabbistir's panel:

- **Install with Homebrew** on a copied `brew install …` command, such as the one in a project's README, or, in Terminal, on a bare package name such as `wget`. It runs `brew install` in the background; the job card shows each step, and a short notice says what was installed.
- **Homebrew updates**, a column of its own that lists your outdated formulae and casks with their versions. ↵ pastes the command that upgrades the one you pick, ⇧↵ pastes its homepage, and ⌘C copies the command.
- **Upgrade all outdated packages**, which runs `brew upgrade` in the background, one step of the bar per package.

## Example

A README says:

```sh
brew install --cask firefox
```

Copy the line, select it in the panel and press ⇧: *Install with Homebrew* is in the list. Press ↵ and the panel closes; the job card under the menu bar icon shows *Starting*, *Downloading*, then *Installing firefox*, and the notice says *Installed firefox.* A `$ ` or `% ` prompt copied with the command is fine, and so is a command split over lines with `\`.

Later, open the panel and move to the *Homebrew updates* column: a row reads *node* with *22.11.0 → 23.3.0 · formula*. ↵ pastes `brew upgrade node` into Terminal, for you to run; type `brew` in the panel and choose *Upgrade all outdated packages* to upgrade everything at once.

## Setup

Install Homebrew with the command from [brew.sh](https://brew.sh), in Terminal:

```sh
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
```

brew cannot install itself, so this is the line yabbistir's Settings shows when brew is missing. Homebrew also has a `.pkg` installer on [its releases page](https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/releases/latest). Without brew, the jobs fail with *brew isn’t installed* and the column cannot list anything.

## Permissions and tools

- **exec**, limited to `brew`. The extension runs exactly these commands, with no shell:
  - `brew install -- <names>` or `brew install --cask -- <names>` for the install actions;
  - `brew outdated --json=v2` for the column, and before *Upgrade all* to know what it will upgrade;
  - `brew info --json=v2 --formula -- <name>` (or `--cask`) when you press ⇧↵ on a row, to read the homepage;
  - `brew upgrade`, with no arguments, for *Upgrade all*.
- **Only package names and `--cask` reach brew.** A copied command is read word by word: `brew install`, then names such as `wget`, `python@3.12` or `hashicorp/tap/terraform`, and `--cask` anywhere. Any other option (`--HEAD`, `--build-from-source`, `--formula`…), a path or a link (`./x.rb`, `https://…`), a file name (`x.rb`, a bottle's `.tar.gz`), quotes, `;`, `&&`, `|`, `$(…)` or a second command, and the action is not offered; if it runs anyway, it does nothing and says why. Names always go after `--`, so none can be read as an option. A row's id is the package's kind and name (and whether it is pinned), checked the same way before it reaches `brew info`.
- **brew can do anything you can.** It downloads from Homebrew's servers and from wherever a formula or cask points, writes into Homebrew's folders and `/Applications`, and a name with a tap (`user/tap/name`) adds that tap from GitHub first and records that package as trusted (in `~/.homebrew/trust.json`), as it would in Terminal. That is why every argument is checked. The extension asks for no network permission of its own.
- **brew's output is read, never shown.** The job card and the notices use the extension's own words; a package's name is the only part of brew's output that reaches them, and only when it looks like a package name. Nothing is logged, and no error message repeats what brew printed.

## How brew runs here

- **It does not stop to ask.** In Terminal, `brew install` and `brew upgrade` show their plan and ask before they go ahead when dependencies are involved. brew skips that question when it is not running in a terminal, as here, so a job goes ahead as `--no-ask` would.
- **It updates itself first, sometimes.** `brew install`, `brew upgrade` and `brew outdated` run `brew update` before their work when the last one was more than a day ago (every five minutes if you set `HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_FROM_API`). That usually takes a few seconds; the job card says *Updating Homebrew* meanwhile. Jobs have no time limit and can be cancelled from their card, which stops brew and everything it started.
- **The column waits up to eight seconds.** A source's list gets ten seconds in all. When `brew outdated` is still updating Homebrew after eight, the column stops it and says *Homebrew is taking too long*, with `brew update` to run in Terminal (↵ or ⌘C copies it). Stopped, the update would start over on the next panel open, so for a minute the column keeps that line without asking brew again. Once you have run `brew update` in Terminal, the column lists your packages quickly again; `HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1` in `brew.env` (next point) avoids the wait altogether.
- **Your shell's `HOMEBREW_*` settings do not reach brew.** yabbistir runs a tool with only `PATH`, `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `USER` and `LANG`. Put the settings you want in `~/.homebrew/brew.env` instead, one `NAME=value` per line, which brew reads itself (as it does `/etc/homebrew/brew.env` and `$(brew --prefix)/etc/homebrew/brew.env`). For example, `HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1` skips the update before every command.

## The column

- It lists what `brew outdated` lists: formulae, and casks except those that update themselves (`auto_updates`) or have no version (`latest`), which `brew outdated --greedy` would add. A pinned package shows *pinned*; *Upgrade all* leaves it as it is, as `brew upgrade` does.
- ↵ pastes the command for just that package, with `--cask` for a cask so that a formula of the same name (such as `docker`) is never meant. For a pinned package it pastes `brew unpin <name> && brew upgrade <name>` (with `--cask` for a cask), the command brew itself suggests, since `brew upgrade` refuses a pinned package: it is only pasted, so you see the unpin before you press return. ⇧↵ pastes the homepage, for both formulae and casks: the place to read what changed before you upgrade. The second action is the same for every row, so its label on the panel's bar always says what it does.
- When nothing is outdated, the column is empty, and the app says so in its own words (*This category is empty.*).
- The list is kept in memory for five minutes and read again after that, and right after any install or upgrade the extension runs. It is never written to disk or yabbistir's history. Its words follow the app's language each time the column opens.

## Limits

- One `brew install` command at a time, with at most 50 package names. A package name with a dot outside its `@` version, or with capital letters, is not taken.
- *Install with Homebrew* on a bare name is offered only when the panel opens over Terminal, on a single word that could be a package name, such as `wget` or `jq`. Elsewhere, ordinary lowercase words, identifiers and branch names would all offer an install. It runs `brew install <name>`, which installs the formula, or the cask when there is no formula of that name; copy `brew install --cask <name>` for a cask that shares a formula's name.
- A cask whose installer asks for your password (many `.pkg` installers do) cannot ask for it here; the job says so, and the command works in Terminal.
- A notice after an install names what was already installed when brew says so, and what brew kept at an older version (a pinned package, or `HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_UPGRADE` in `brew.env`); otherwise every name counts as installed. After *Upgrade all*, the notice names what brew started to upgrade, and the rest as not upgraded.
- brew's notes after an install or upgrade (caveats: a PATH line for a keg-only formula, `brew services start …`, a restart some casks need) are not shown. When brew printed some, the notice after an install says so; `brew info <name>` prints them.
