# Kubernetes

The pods of your current Kubernetes context as a column in yabbistir's panel, through [kubectl](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/). Each row is a pod: its name, and a quieter line with its namespace, status, ready containers and the context. ↵ pastes the pod name, ⇧↵ pastes `kubectl -n <namespace> logs -f <pod>`, and ⌘C copies the pod name.

## Example

Type `api` in the *Pods* column to find `api-7d9f-xk2lp` (`web · Running 2/2 · kind-demo`). ↵ pastes `api-7d9f-xk2lp`; ⇧↵ pastes `kubectl -n web logs -f api-7d9f-xk2lp`, ready for you to press Return in Terminal.

## Setup

```sh
brew install kubectl
```

The extension uses whatever context kubectl has selected (`kubectl config use-context <name>`), and your own kubeconfig. It never signs in for you: when the column says the cluster can't be reached or kubectl isn't signed in, fix that in Terminal first. If it says your account can't list pods (Forbidden), you are signed in but not allowed to; try the Namespace setting or ask the cluster's owner.

## Settings

- **Namespace**: empty lists every namespace (`--all-namespaces`); a name lists only that namespace.
- **⇧↵ pastes**: `kubectl logs -f` (default) or `kubectl exec -it … -- sh`.

## Permissions and tools

- `exec`, to run **kubectl** and nothing else, with fixed arguments: `kubectl config current-context` and `kubectl get pods --output json --chunk-size=0 --request-timeout=6s` with `--all-namespaces` or `--namespace <name>`. The namespace from Settings is checked to be a valid name first. Pasting a command only pastes text; the extension never runs `logs` or `exec` itself.
- No `network` permission: kubectl talks to the cluster, not the extension.

## Limits

- The column shows at most 300 pods, sorted by namespace then name. Narrow it with the Namespace setting, or search.
- Only the current context is read, and the pasted command does not name it. Switch context before running the command.
- Status is a short version of kubectl's STATUS column (for example `CrashLoopBackOff`, `Terminating`, `Completed`, `Init:Error`); it can differ from kubectl in rare cases.
- The context name is shown in every row's subtitle as kubectl reports it. Cloud contexts (EKS, GKE) often contain an account or project id, so mind a screen share.
- Pods are read again each time the panel opens (a request gives up after 6 seconds); nothing is kept. The listing has 10 seconds in all, shared by reading the context, the request and parsing; on a very large or slow cluster it can run out and show an error instead.
- Messages never include kubectl's output, since it can name users and servers.

Sources: kubectl reference for [`get`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_get/) and [`config current-context`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_config/kubectl_config_current-context/). Error wording (`current-context is not set`, `Unable to connect to the server`, `You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)`, `Forbidden`) is from kubectl's behavior as widely documented, not from running it.

# Recent Projects

The folders and workspaces you opened lately in VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, VSCodium or VS Code Insiders, as a column in yabbistir's panel. Each row shows the project's name, the editor and where it is. ↵ pastes the project's path, ⇧↵ pastes the editor's command that opens it, and ⌘C copies the path.

## Example

You are in a terminal and want to `cd` into a project you had open in VS Code this morning. Open the panel, move to the *Recent projects* column and type `shop`:

| Row | Second line |
|---|---|
| shop | VS Code · ~/dev/shop |
| Shop Admin | Cursor · ~/clients/Shop Admin |

Press ↵ on *shop* and `/Users/you/dev/shop` is pasted after your `cd `. Press ⇧↵ instead and the command that opens it in its editor is pasted, ready to run:

```sh
code /Users/you/dev/shop
cursor '/Users/you/clients/Shop Admin'
```

A path with spaces or other characters a shell treats specially is put in single quotes in the command. The path ↵ pastes is always as it is, for a chat, a file dialog or a quoted argument.

## What is listed

- **Folders and workspaces** (`.code-workspace` files), never single files. A workspace's row shows its name without `.code-workspace`.
- **Up to 50 projects**, newest first. When you use more than one editor, their lists are taken in turns, starting with the editor you started last: its newest, then the next editor's newest, then each one's second newest, and so on. The editors keep no date with a list's entries, only an order, but each writes down when it last started; this is the closest the column can come to one timeline. An editor that does not say when it started comes after the others.
- **Each project once.** A folder you opened in both VS Code and Cursor appears once, at the higher of its two places, under the editor you started more recently: that is the editor its second line names and ⇧↵ opens it in. On your Mac, paths that differ only in letter case or in how an accented letter is stored count as one, as they do on the Mac's disk.
- **Remote projects** too: a folder on an SSH host, in a dev container, through a tunnel or in a codespace. The second line says where it is (*VS Code · SSH: build-box · /home/you/api*). ↵ pastes its path on that machine, and ⇧↵ a command that opens it with the editor's `--folder-uri` (or `--file-uri` for a workspace), for example `code --folder-uri vscode-remote://ssh-remote%2Bbuild-box/home/you/api`.
- **Virtual projects**, such as a GitHub repository opened without cloning it. The second line shows its address (*VS Code · vscode-vfs://github/you/site*), without the branch or pull request GitHub writes into it after a `+`. ↵ pastes the whole address, since it has no path on a disk, and ⇧↵ the command that opens it.

Left out: the editors' untitled workspaces, network shares written the Windows way, and any path with a line break or another control character in it, so a pasted path never runs a command on its own in a terminal.

An editor that is not installed, or has not opened anything yet, adds nothing. With no projects at all, the column is empty.

## Setup

Nothing to set up for ↵: the column fills as soon as the extension is installed. `sqlite3` comes with macOS, so there is nothing to install either.

For ⇧↵, the editor's command must be in your PATH: `code` for VS Code, `code-insiders` for VS Code Insiders, `cursor` for Cursor, `windsurf` for Windsurf and `codium` for VSCodium. Each editor installs its own: open its Command Palette (⇧⌘P), type `shell command` and choose the command that installs it in PATH ([VS Code's guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/mac#_launch-vs-code-from-the-command-line)). Then open a new terminal window.

## Settings

- **Home folder**: where the editors' data is looked for. It is filled in for you (`~`, your home folder), and there is nothing to change unless you keep your editors' data under another user's folder. The extension needs it because a program it runs gets only an absolute path, and an extension learns the home folder's path from a folder setting like this one. When it is cleared, the column asks you to choose it again.

## Where the lists come from

VS Code and the editors built from it keep the recent list as JSON, under the key `history.recentlyOpenedPathsList`, in an SQLite database. The extension looks in two places for each editor, in this order:

1. `~/Library/Application Support/<editor>/User/globalStorage/state.vscdb`, where the list is kept up to VS Code 1.117, and where each editor keeps its other state. When this file is not there, the editor is not installed and nothing else is read for it.
2. `~/<shared folder>/sharedStorage/state.vscdb`, where VS Code 1.118 and later move the list: `~/.vscode-shared` for VS Code, `~/.vscode-insiders-shared` for VS Code Insiders and `~/.vscode-oss-shared` for VSCodium.

The `<editor>` folders are `Code`, `Code - Insiders`, `Cursor`, `Windsurf` and `VSCodium`. Cursor and Windsurf keep their list in the first place today; for when they move to VS Code 1.118 or later, the extension also looks in `~/.cursor-shared` and `~/.windsurf-shared`, following VS Code's naming.

From the first database the extension also reads `telemetry.currentSessionDate`: the date the editor last started, which it writes there each time it starts, whatever its telemetry setting. It decides which editor's list comes first.

The lists are read again each time the panel opens, so a folder you just opened is there the next time, and again when you press ↵ or ⇧↵ on a row. Nothing is ever written to these files. An editor that keeps its database in WAL mode leaves it unreadable to a read-only program while the editor is closed; the extension then reads the file as it is on disk.

Sources: VS Code's [recent list](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/platform/workspaces/electron-main/workspacesHistoryMainService.ts) and [its format](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/platform/workspaces/common/workspaces.ts), the [database's table](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/base/parts/storage/node/storage.ts), the [start date](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/platform/storage/electron-main/storageMain.ts), and the [shared storage](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/311317) of VS Code 1.118.

## Permissions and privacy

- **exec**, limited to `sqlite3`, which comes with macOS (`/usr/bin/sqlite3`). The extension runs it with fixed options and one fixed query: `-readonly` (it can neither change the database nor create one that is missing), `-safe` (no SQL or command that reads other files, writes files or runs a program), `-init /dev/null` (your `~/.sqliterc` is not read), and `--` before the database's path, so the path is never taken for an option. When a database cannot be opened that way, it is asked for once more as `file:…?immutable=1`, still read-only, which opens a WAL database whose editor is closed; a missing database stays missing. The path is built from the home folder setting and the fixed names above. yabbistir tells you before install that the extension "Can run these programs on your Mac: sqlite3. They can read and write your files and reach the internet"; this extension uses it only to read the two databases per editor named above.
- **Only the recent list and the start date are read.** The query takes the two keys above and nothing else from the editors' databases; of each entry it uses the folder's or workspace's address, never its label or any other field.
- **Nothing is stored or sent.** No network permission; nothing is written to the extension's storage or to a file, and the extension keeps nothing in memory between calls: ↵ and ⇧↵ read the row's editor's list again to find its project. yabbistir keeps the rows in memory until the Mac locks or sleeps or the app quits. They never reach yabbistir's history, its search index or the disk.
- **Nothing about your projects is logged.** The Development log says once, naming only the editor, when an editor's database is there but cannot be read, and when an editor's database holds no recent list and it has no shared one, which can mean that its list moved somewhere this version does not know.

## Limits

- The order across editors is by turns, the editor started last first, not by the time each project was opened (see *What is listed*). An editor left running for days counts from the day it started.
- Cursor's and Windsurf's shared folders are not published yet. If either moves its list somewhere else than `~/.cursor-shared` or `~/.windsurf-shared`, its projects stop showing until the extension learns the new place, and the Development log says that no recent list was found for it. The editor's `product.json` names the place (`sharedDataFolderName`, in `/Applications/Cursor.app/Contents/Resources/app/product.json` for Cursor).
- A source cannot open a link or an app in yabbistir, so ⇧↵ pastes the command rather than opening the project itself. Run it in a terminal.
- Editors older than VS Code 1.55 kept the list in another shape, and still older ones in another file; those lists are not read.
- The list is read only for the editors above, in their usual folders. An editor started with its own `--user-data-dir` keeps its list elsewhere.

# Password Generator

Makes a strong password or a random key right where you type. Open the panel (⇧⌘V), type `password`, `passphrase`, `pin` or `key`, and the row already shows the value that ↵ will paste.

| Row | What you get | Settings |
|---|---|---|
| Generate a password | Random characters, at least one from every set that is on | Length 8 to 128 (default 20); lowercase, uppercase, digits, symbols; leave out look-alikes `I l 1 O 0` (on by default) |
| Generate a passphrase | Random words from the EFF large word list | 4 to 8 words (default 5); separator: dash, space, period, underscore, comma or none |
| Generate a PIN | Digits only | 4 to 12 digits (default 6) |
| Generate a hex key | 32 random bytes as 64 lowercase hex digits | none |
| Generate a Base64URL key | 32 random bytes as 43 characters, no padding | none |

## Example

With the defaults, *Generate a password* shows something like `q7Rm-xW3#tBv9Kd2Zn_p`, and *Generate a passphrase* something like `crunching-oyster-pledge-bonus-jogger` (five words, about 64 bits).

## How the values are made

- The only source of randomness is `crypto.getRandomValues`. `Math.random` is never used.
- Every pick from a list uses **rejection sampling**: a 32-bit draw that falls in the last, incomplete block is thrown away, so every single pick is unbiased (no modulo bias). A password also guarantees one character from each enabled set, then fills the rest from the whole pool. The password is then shuffled with an unbiased Fisher-Yates shuffle.
- Every character set that is on is present in the password.
- The row's hint and the pasted value are the same run: what you see is what ↵ pastes.
- Four EFF words contain a hyphen themselves (`drop-down`, `felt-tip`, `t-shirt`, `yo-yo`); with the dash separator they look like two words. Pick another separator if that matters to you.

## Permissions

None. It needs no network, runs no program, and reads no clipboard history. It never logs or shows a generated value anywhere but in the result.

## Limits

- yabbistir has no way for an extension to mark a result as concealed or keep it out of history. **A generated value is pasted like any text and joins clipboard history**, where anyone with access to your history can read it. Delete the item from history after you have used a password that matters.
- Length, word count and PIN length are set in Settings, not in the row. A length that is not a whole number falls back to 20, and one outside 8 to 128 is moved to the nearest end.
- If all four character sets are turned off, the row says so and pastes nothing.

## Word list

The passphrase words are the EFF large word list (7,776 words), unchanged, from <https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2016/07/new-wordlists-random-passphrases>. Copyright Electronic Frontier Foundation, licensed under [Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 United States (CC BY 3.0 US)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/us/). The list is in `src/words.ts`.

## Develop

```sh
npm test -- dev.yabbistir.password-generator
npm run build -- dev.yabbistir.password-generator
```

# 1Password

Your 1Password logins as columns in yabbistir's panel, through [op](https://developer.1password.com/docs/cli/), 1Password's command-line tool, signed in by the 1Password app. The *1Password* column lists your Login items: each row shows the item's name, with its username and website below. ↵ pastes the password, ⇧↵ pastes the username, and ⌘C copies the username. The *1Password codes* column lists the same logins: ↵ pastes the item's current one-time code.

## Example

Click into a login form's password field, open the panel and move to the *1Password* column. Type `posta` to find *Posta* (`deniz.k@ornek.dev · posta.ornek.dev`) and press ↵: the password is pasted, and your clipboard comes back a moment later. When the site then asks for a code, open the panel again, move to *1Password codes*, find *Posta* and press ↵.

## Setup

1. Install op:

   ```sh
   brew install 1password-cli
   ```

2. Open and unlock the 1Password app, and turn on **Settings › Developer › Integrate with 1Password CLI**. Turning on Touch ID in 1Password lets you approve with your fingerprint.
3. On macOS 27, also open **System Settings › Privacy & Security › Files & Folders**, find yabbistir, and turn on the setting that starts with *Data shared by 1Password*. Without it, op answers as if the integration were off.
4. Open the *1Password* column. 1Password asks you to allow access: approve it.

op 2.30.0 or later is needed. When the column says *op needs an update*, press ↵ or ⌘C on that row to copy `brew upgrade 1password-cli`, and run it in Terminal.

The extension only works through the 1Password app: it never asks for, sees or keeps your account password, and it does not use `op signin` sessions or service account tokens.

## Approving and locking

1Password decides when to ask, not the extension. For Terminal, 1Password documents that an approval lasts until 1Password locks, through 10 minutes without use, and for 12 hours at most. Expect something like it for yabbistir: 1Password usually doesn't ask again for about 10 minutes of use, and asks again after it locks, the next time a column lists or you pick a row.

When 1Password is locked or you dismiss its prompt, the column shows *1Password is locked or didn’t allow access* and its rows go. Unlock 1Password, then open the column again. When op cannot reach the app at all (the integration is off, 1Password is not running, or macOS 27 has not allowed yabbistir), the column says where to turn the integration on. When the Mac is offline, it says so.

The extension stops op after about eight seconds, inside yabbistir's 10-second limit. If 1Password's prompt is still waiting by then, the column says that 1Password didn't answer in time: approve the prompt, then open the column again. If you unlock 1Password by typing your account password, unlock it first, then open the column: typing can take longer than the column waits.

## Settings

- **Account**: for people with more than one 1Password account. Its sign-in address, such as `my.1password.com`, or its ID, as `op account list` shows them. Leave it empty to use the account op used last.
- **Vault**: to list one vault only, by its name or ID. Leave it empty to list every vault.

## What is listed

Login items from every vault the 1Password app has for the account, or only the chosen vault; archived items are left out. Favorites come first, then the rest by name. A row's second line is the item's username and its website's host; a user name or password written into the website's link is never shown.

The extension may reuse its list for up to five minutes. Before it does, it runs `op whoami`, which never shows a prompt. When that fails (1Password has locked since, or op has not been approved for yabbistir), the rows go and the list is read again. An item you add or change in 1Password shows up within five minutes at most.

## One-time codes

A column offers the same actions on every row, and op's list does not say which items have a one-time code. So the codes are a column of their own, listing every login: ↵ on an item without a one-time password says *This item has no one-time code*.

Like every column an extension adds, both columns show when you pick them, and list as they open. In Settings › Categories you can set either to show always; then it lists each time the panel opens, and 1Password may ask for approval then. Two columns that open together share one `op item list`, and so one prompt.

## Permissions and privacy

- **exec**, limited to `op`. The extension runs `op --version`, `op whoami`, `op item list --categories Login --format json` and `op item get` with fixed options. The only other arguments are an item's id, which must be letters and digits before it reaches op, and the account and vault from Settings, each passed as one `--account=…` or `--vault=…` argument so they can never be read as another option. It never uses op's options that share, edit or copy items, and it asks for no network permission.
- **op can read every vault the 1Password app opens for it.** For the list, the extension reads each Login item's id, name, category, favorite mark, username and website, never its fields. It reads one field (`op item get --fields label=password` or `label=username`), or the current code (`op item get --otp`), only when you press ↵, ⇧↵ or ⌘C on a row. The code is the one op works out; the secret behind it never reaches the extension.
- **Passwords and codes are never stored or shown.** Not in yabbistir's history, not in the extension's storage or a file, not in a log and not in an error message. yabbistir pastes them as one item for this Mac only, marked so that clipboard managers (its own history included) skip it, and gives your clipboard back a moment later. When it cannot paste, without Accessibility access for example, it leaves the value on the clipboard for 30 seconds and says so.
- **An empty password, username or code is never pasted.** The extension says the item has none instead.
- **op's own messages never reach yours.** The extension reads op's errors only to choose one of its own messages, and never shows, logs or keeps them.
- **The list stays in memory only.** The extension reuses its list for up to five minutes, and yabbistir keeps the rows in memory until the Mac locks or sleeps, the column next finds 1Password locked, or the app quits. They never reach yabbistir's history, its search index or the disk.

Because it can paste secrets, the extension is marked sensitive. Before you install it, yabbistir tells you it "Can read and paste secrets such as passwords. They’re never written to history or disk."

## Limits

- Login items only: passwords kept as *Password*, *API Credential* or other categories are not listed.
- One account at a time: the one in Settings, or the one op used last.
- Very large vaults may not list within yabbistir's 10 seconds. Then the column says that 1Password took too long: choose one vault in Settings to list fewer.
- op's messages are in English and may change between versions. The extension recognizes a locked app, a dismissed prompt, a missing integration, the Mac being offline, an unknown vault or account, and an item without a password, username or one-time code from op's own words, never from the names op quotes in them. Any other failure says that op could not list or read, without op's own text.

## Troubleshooting

- *Open 1Password and turn on “Integrate with 1Password CLI”* although it is on: on macOS 27, allow yabbistir under System Settings › Privacy & Security › Files & Folders (*Data shared by 1Password*). Otherwise, keep 1Password running, or restart it.
- *1Password took too long to list your logins*: choose one vault in Settings.
- *1Password didn’t answer in time*: approve 1Password's prompt, or unlock 1Password first, then open the column again.

# Linear

Your open Linear issues as a column in yabbistir's panel, a copied issue key turned into a link, and a copied error turned into a new issue.

- **The Linear column** lists the issues assigned to you that are not done, canceled or a duplicate, most recently updated first, up to 50. A row reads *ENG-123 Login button does nothing on Safari*, with *In Progress · Engineering · High* under it. ↵ pastes the issue's link, ⇧↵ pastes a Markdown link, `[ENG-123: Login button does nothing on Safari](https://linear.app/…)`, and ⌘C copies the link.
- **Paste as Linear link** is offered on a copied issue key such as `ENG-123`, and on a link to an issue in Linear. It looks the issue up and pastes the Markdown link with its title.
- **Create Linear issue from this** is offered on copied text. It makes a new issue from it in your team, pastes the new issue's link, and says *ENG-124 created in Linear.*

## Example

A test fails in Terminal. Copy what it printed:

```text
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
    at renderList (app.js:12:9)
    at main (app.js:40:3)
```

Click into your chat with the team, open the panel, type `linear` and pick *Create Linear issue from this*. Linear gets an issue titled *TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')*, with the whole trace in a code block as its description, and its link is pasted into the chat.

Later, someone writes "is ENG-124 fixed?". Copy `ENG-124`, open the panel, press ⇧ on the copy and pick *Paste as Linear link*: `[ENG-124: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')](https://linear.app/…)` is pasted.

## Setup

1. In Linear, open **Settings › Account › Security & access** and create a key under **Personal API keys**. The least it needs is two permissions: **Read**, for the column, the links and finding your team, and **Create issues**, for new issues. Full access works too, but gives the key more than the extension uses. A key limited to some teams sees, and creates, issues in those teams only. If you are a member rather than an admin and can't make a key, a workspace admin has to allow it first, under **Settings › Administration › API › Member API keys**.
2. In yabbistir, open **Settings → Extensions → Linear** and paste the key into **API key**.
3. Optionally, fill in **Team key for new issues** with the key your team's issues start with, such as `ENG`. Left empty, new issues go to your team when you are in only one; when you are in several, the action asks you to choose.

Until there is a key, the column shows one row asking for it. ↵ or ⌘C on it copies `open https://linear.app/settings/account/security`, which opens Linear's API-key page when you run it in Terminal.

## How a copy becomes an issue

- **Title:** the first line that has a letter or a digit. Code fences are skipped, and a Markdown heading's `#` and a log line's time stamp are left out. When only a fence line has words, as in ```` ```Error in prod ````, the title is those words. Runs of spaces become one, and a title over 100 characters is cut at a word, with "…".
- **Description:** the whole copy, without blank lines at its ends. It goes in a code block when yabbistir took the copy for code, or when it reads as code, a log or a stack trace:
  - a single line such as `TypeError: …` or `2026-11-04 08:12:03 ERROR …`;
  - two lines that both look like code, or one of them a stack frame, a log line, a prompt such as `$ npm test`, or an indented line;
  - three lines or more, at least half of which look like code, log lines, stack frames or indented code.

  Indented list items, such as `  1. Open the panel` or `  - Press return`, count as prose. Anything else is kept as it is, and Linear reads it as Markdown. A description over 50,000 characters, its code block's fences included, is cut at a line, with a note under it saying so.
- **Everything else** is the team's default: the issue has no assignee, labels, project or priority, and starts in the team's default state.

## Permissions and privacy

- **network**, limited to `api.linear.app`, Linear's API. It is reached only when you open the panel or choose an action, and only for this:
  - Opening the panel, when the column's list is over a minute old: one request for your open issues. After a failed request the column waits a minute before asking again, or, after a rate limit, as long as Linear asks.
  - ↵, ⇧↵ or ⌘C on a row: the issue's id, to get its current link and title.
  - *Paste as Linear link*: the issue key you copied.
  - *Create Linear issue from this*: the team key from Settings (or a request for your teams, when it is empty), then the new issue's title and description, made from the copy you chose.
- **The API key** is kept in the macOS Keychain by yabbistir. The extension reads it only to make a request, sends it only to `api.linear.app`, as the request's Authorization header, and never logs it, keeps it or puts it in a message. Messages are the extension's own words; Linear's error texts are never shown.
- **Rows stay in memory.** The extension reuses its list for up to a minute, remembering only a fingerprint of the key it was made with, so a new key never shows the old key's issues. yabbistir keeps the rows in memory until the Mac locks or sleeps or the app quits; they never reach yabbistir's history, its search index or the disk. A row's link is fetched when you pick it and not kept.
- **Nothing runs on its own.** Neither action runs as a hint, so nothing is sent until you choose one.

## Limits

- The column shows at most 50 issues, and only those assigned to you.
- *Paste as Linear link* takes the whole copy as a key: two to ten capital letters and digits starting with a letter, a dash and up to six digits (`ENG-123`), or a `https://linear.app/<workspace>/issue/ENG-123/…` link. A lowercase key, or one inside a sentence, is not offered.
- New issues go to one team: the one in Settings, or your only one.
- Linear allows each Linear user 2,500 requests an hour, shared by all their API keys and the other tools that use them. The column asks at most once a minute, after a failure too; when Linear limits you anyway, it waits until Linear takes requests again (three minutes when Linear doesn't say), and its message says when to try again.
- If creating an issue times out or is cancelled, Linear may have made it all the same: check Linear before trying again, or there will be two.
- Telling code from prose is a guess from the copy's first 300 lines. A message with one stack frame in a paragraph stays prose.
- The 50,000-character limit on a description is the extension's own, to keep requests small; Linear documents none.
- A code block's fence is longer than any run of backticks in the copy, up to 32 of them, so only a copy with 32 or more backticks in a row can end its code block early.

## Sources

- Linear's GraphQL API: [authentication, queries and errors](https://linear.app/developers/graphql), [rate limiting](https://linear.app/developers/rate-limiting), [pagination](https://linear.app/developers/pagination) and [filtering](https://linear.app/developers/filtering).
- Personal API keys, their permissions and the admin setting for member keys: Linear's [API and webhooks](https://linear.app/docs/api-and-webhooks) page.
- The error types for a plan's limits (`usage limit exceeded`, `feature not accessible`): Linear's SDK, [`error.ts`](https://github.com/linear/linear/blob/master/packages/sdk/src/error.ts).
- Field names, filters and the workflow state types (`completed`, `canceled`, `duplicate`): Linear's public [GraphQL schema](https://github.com/linear/linear/blob/master/packages/sdk/src/schema.graphql).

# SSH Hosts

The hosts in your SSH config as a column in yabbistir's panel. Each row shows a host's alias and, quieter, `user@hostname:port` (parts the config does not set are left out). ↵ pastes `ssh <alias>`, ⇧↵ pastes the full command, and ⌘C copies `ssh <alias>`.

## Example

With this in `~/.ssh/config`:

```text
Host prod-db
    HostName db.example.test
    User deploy
    Port 2222
```

open the panel in Terminal, move to the *SSH Hosts* column and type `prod`. The row reads *prod-db* with `deploy@db.example.test:2222` under it. ↵ pastes `ssh prod-db`; ⇧↵ pastes `ssh deploy@db.example.test -p 2222`. Neither presses Return for you.

## Setup

1. Open Settings → Extensions → SSH Hosts and choose the **SSH folder**. The folder is `.ssh` in your home folder, which macOS hides. In the picker press ⌘⇧. (Command-Shift-Period) to show hidden folders, then choose `.ssh`.
2. Open the panel and move to the SSH Hosts column. Until a folder is chosen, or when it has no `config` file or no hosts, the column says what to do.

## What it reads

- The `config` file in the folder you chose, and nothing else: no keys, no `known_hosts`.
- `Host` blocks, with `HostName`, `User` and `Port`. A `Host` line with several names gives one row each. Patterns (names with `*`, `?` or `!`, such as `Host *`) are skipped, and so are their options. Option names are not case sensitive, `Option=value` works, and values may be in double quotes.
- Like ssh, the first value of an option wins when a host appears twice.
- `Match` blocks are ignored.
- `Include` lines that name a file inside the same folder, relative (`Include work`) or absolute (`Include /Users/you/.ssh/work`), and `~/.ssh/work` when the folder you chose is `.ssh`. Includes inside included files are followed up to eight levels deep.
- **Limit:** a config that is a symlink pointing out of the folder, or cannot be read, counts as missing. Host names with spaces or a leading dash get no row; when that leaves nothing, the column says so.
- **Limit:** the extension cannot list a folder, so a glob such as `Include config.d/*` is not followed; name the files one by one. Files outside the chosen folder are never read.
- Options from `Host *` blocks are not merged into the rows; ssh still applies them when you run the command.

## What is pasted

- ↵ pastes `ssh <alias>`, which uses everything in your config.
- ⇧↵ pastes `ssh user@hostname -p port` using the host's own options (parts that are not set are left out). yabbistir cannot open a link in your terminal (`yab.open` opens only web links, and not from a column), so this is the way to get the details in front of ssh.
- Only plain names reach the pasted line. An alias, host name, user or port with spaces, quotes, `;`, `$` or a leading `-` is not pasted: such an alias gets no row, and for the other values ⇧↵ falls back to `ssh <alias>`. `%h` in a `HostName` is read as the alias; other `%` tokens are not supported.

## Permissions and privacy

None. Reading the folder you chose needs no permission; the app only lets the extension read inside the folder you picked in Settings. The extension cannot write there, runs no program, and uses no network.

Rows stay in memory only; the extension stores nothing and logs nothing. The config is read again each time the panel opens and each time you paste or copy a row.

# Link Tools

Shows where an is.gd or v.gd short link really goes before you open or paste it, and makes short links when you need one.

- **Expand short link**: on an is.gd or v.gd link, returns the destination as text, so ↵ pastes the real address. It follows up to 5 hops while the next hop is still an is.gd or v.gd link.
- **Shorten with is.gd**: on any web link, returns a short `https://is.gd/…` link. Links that are already short, or that contain a username or password, are not sent.
- **Short link** tag: a small chip on is.gd and v.gd links, so the expand action is easy to find. The detector makes no network request.

## Example

Copy `https://is.gd/Ab12`, choose *Expand short link*: `https://example.org/article?id=7` is what ↵ pastes.
Copy `https://example.org/a/very/long/address`, choose *Shorten with is.gd*: `https://is.gd/Q7xK2m`.

## Permission: network

Only `is.gd` and `v.gd` are reachable. Reasons:

- Expanding asks is.gd or v.gd's documented lookup API where the short link goes. The short link is the only thing sent.
- Shortening sends the link you chose to `is.gd`, which is what the action is for. Never run it on a link that contains a secret: is.gd keeps the link.
- Nothing else is sent, and nothing is stored or logged. Error messages never contain the link.

## Setup

None. No tools to install.

## Limits

- **Only is.gd and v.gd.** yabbistir holds every request, redirects included, to the extension's `network.domains` and rejects a redirect that leaves the list. A shortener such as bit.ly answers with a redirect to an outside destination, so it cannot be read this way. Instead of an action that nearly always fails, Link Tools expands only the two services with a documented lookup API (`forward.php`).
- If the destination is another shortener (for example bit.ly), that address is returned as is.
- Only `http` and `https` destinations are returned. A destination that is anything else is refused.
- More than 5 hops, or a loop, ends with a message.
- Expanding does not check whether the destination is safe.
- is.gd limits how often it can be called; a busy answer says "try again in a minute".

## Sources

- is.gd create API: https://is.gd/apishorteningreference.php
- is.gd lookup API: https://is.gd/apilookupreference.php

# Send To

Sends what you copied to a notes or task app without switching to it. Copy text or a link, open the actions and choose *Send to Things* (or Obsidian, Bear, Drafts, OmniFocus, Reminders, Notes). Nothing is pasted: a short notice says "Sent to Things".

## Example

Copy `Buy oat milk` followed by a second line `two cartons`, choose *Send to Things*. A to-do titled "Buy oat milk" with the notes "two cartons" appears in the Things Inbox.

| Destination | What is created | How |
|---|---|---|
| Obsidian | A note named after the first line; the whole text is its content. Settings can name a vault and a folder. | `obsidian://new` with `vault`, `name` or `file`, `content` |
| Things | A to-do in the Inbox: first line is the title, the rest the notes. | `things:///add` with `title`, `notes` |
| Bear | A note with the whole text (Bear takes its title from the first line). It is created without opening Bear's window. | `bear://x-callback-url/create` with `text`, `open_note=no`, `show_window=no` |
| Drafts | A draft with the whole text. | `drafts://create` with `text` |
| OmniFocus | An Inbox item: first line is the name, the rest the note. | `omnifocus:///add` with `name`, `note`, `autosave=true` |
| Apple Reminders | A reminder in your default list: first line is the title, the rest the notes. | AppleScript through `osascript` |
| Apple Notes | A note; the first line becomes a heading. | AppleScript through `osascript` |

A link is sent as its address.

## Permissions and tools

- **exec**, limited to two programs that ship with macOS:
  - `open`, to open the destination app's URL. yabbistir's own `yab.open` opens only http and https links, so an app's own scheme (`things:///…`) needs `open`. The extension passes `-g` (stay in the background) and one argument, a URL the extension built itself that always starts with one of the five fixed schemes above, so it can never be read as an option.
  - `osascript`, only for Reminders and Notes. The AppleScript is a fixed text inside the extension. Your text is passed as separate arguments, each prefixed with a letter that the script removes, so quotes, backslashes and AppleScript keywords in it are plain data, never code.
- No network permission. Your text goes only to the app you chose, on this Mac.

Nothing to install: both tools are part of macOS.

## Setup

1. Open the extension's settings and turn on the destinations you use. Reminders and Notes are off by default because macOS asks for permission the first time.
2. Optional: set the Obsidian vault name (Obsidian uses the vault you last had open when this is empty) and a folder inside the vault, such as `Inbox/Clips`.
3. The first time you use Reminders or Notes, macOS asks whether yabbistir may control it. Allow it (System Settings › Privacy & Security › Automation). If the question stays open longer than ten seconds the first send may time out; just send again.

## Limits

- Turning a destination off in settings does not hide its row: the manifest format has no per-variant visibility field, so all seven rows are always listed and a disabled one answers "turned off" without doing anything. Reminders and Notes are off by default, so they show up as rows that ask you to turn them on first.
- Reminders and Notes need yabbistir 0.4.1 or later. Earlier versions can't ask macOS for Automation access: macOS refuses the request without asking, and yabbistir doesn't show up in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Automation. The other five destinations work on 0.3.0 and later.
- Reminders and Notes use `osascript`, which `docs/review-checklist.md` lists among shells. It is a constant script with your text passed only as arguments (no injection is possible); if a maintainer rejects it, the fallback is to drop those two destinations.
- OmniFocus: `name`, `note` and `autosave=true` come from community write-ups, not an official page. If OmniFocus ignores `autosave`, the item may wait as an unsaved draft in the Inbox.
- An encoded URL is cut to 30,000 characters (our own conservative limit: the apps' documents name no limit except Things' notes, 10,000 characters). Cut text ends with an ellipsis and the notice says "cut to fit".
- Things: titles are cut to 250 characters; when the first line is longer, the whole text goes in the notes.
- Obsidian: file-name characters Obsidian forbids are replaced by spaces; if a note with that name exists, Obsidian decides what happens. When the first line is empty of usable characters, the name is "Clipboard <date> <time>".
- Notes and Reminders get at most 100,000 characters.
- The extension cannot tell whether an app actually saved the item: `open` reports only whether the URL could be handed to an app. If none handles the scheme it says the app could not be reached.

## Sources

URL scheme parameters come from each app's documentation: Things URL Scheme (culturedcode.com/things/support/articles/2803573), Obsidian URI (obsidian.md/help/Extending+Obsidian/Obsidian+URI), Bear x-callback-url (bear.app/faq/x-callback-url-scheme-documentation), Drafts URL Schemes (docs.getdrafts.com/docs/automation/urlschemes). OmniFocus does not publish a page we could reach; `name`, `note` and `autosave=true` follow its documented iOS and Mac URL scheme as described in community write-ups (learnomnifocus.com, Omni Group forums).

# Safe Paste

Paste without surprises. Safe Paste spots what a copy hides, tells you in plain words, and pastes a cleaned version where it matters most: in a terminal.

## Why

A web page can put a different command on your clipboard than the one you saw. Text can carry characters you cannot see (zero-width spaces, direction overrides) that change what a command or an address really is. A final newline makes a terminal run a command the moment it lands. yabbistir knows which app a paste is headed for, so Safe Paste can offer the safe version first when that app is a terminal.

## What it does

**Three tags**, shown as chips on a copy, each with a short explanation in its preview:

- **Hidden characters**: zero-width characters, direction controls (the "Trojan Source" trick), soft hyphens, control characters such as escape and backspace, and blank-looking letters. The preview counts each kind, says on which lines (or at which positions) they are, and shows the text with each one made visible. A joiner inside an emoji sequence, a half-space in Persian, a direction mark inside Hebrew or Arabic and the tag characters of a flag emoji are normal and are not reported.
- **Look-alike letters**: a word that mixes Latin letters with Cyrillic or Greek ones that look the same (`p` + Cyrillic `а` + `ypal`), and, in an address, a part made only of such letters next to a plain Latin part. Text written entirely in Cyrillic or Greek is never reported.
- **Risky command**: a download piped into a shell (`curl … | sh`, `bash <(curl …)`), decoded text run as a script (`base64 -d | sh`), `sudo`, `rm -r` aimed at a whole disk of files (`/`, `/*`, `~`, `~/*`, `$HOME`, `*`, `.`, `..`; an ordinary path such as `/tmp/build` or `~/proj/node_modules` is not tagged), a fork bomb, `chmod -R 777`, and appending to a shell startup file (`>> ~/.zshrc`). The preview names the kind of risk and the line, never the command itself, and adds when the paste ends with a newline, holds several commands or contains curly quotes or a look-alike dash before an option (which shells do not read as quotes or options). The Look-alike and Hidden previews say the same. A plain command is not tagged.

**Two actions:**

- **Paste safely** (leads in terminals): removes the hidden characters, turns non-breaking and other odd spaces into plain spaces, line endings into `\n`, and strips newlines, spaces and tabs at the very end of the text (a space escaped by a backslash stays). Quotes, trailing spaces inside the text and everything else are left alone. The row shows exactly what is pasted; when nothing needs changing, the text pastes as it is. It never fixes a dangerous command, it only removes what is hidden, so you can read it and decide.
- **Remove hidden characters** (offered on copies tagged "Hidden characters"): the same hidden-character cleanup and nothing else, for editors and browsers where quotes, spaces and newlines matter.

## Example

You copy a one-line install command from a page. It looks like `curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh`, but a zero-width space sits after `curl` and a newline ends it. The copy gets the "Hidden characters" and "Risky command" chips. In a terminal, "Paste safely" is first in the list and shows `curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` without the hidden character and without the newline, so you read it and press return yourself.

## Permissions

None. The extension only reads the copy it is asked about. It uses no network, runs no program and writes nothing; nothing is logged.

## Setup

Install it. There is nothing to set up.

## Limits

- Detection reads words, not the whole shell language: it will miss a danger hidden behind variables, functions or aliases, and a quoted `|` can look like a pipe. It is a second pair of eyes, not a guarantee.
- Look-alike detection knows the Cyrillic and Greek letters that are drawn like Latin ones. A word made only of such letters (all Cyrillic `аррӏе`) is reported only inside a dotted address next to a plain Latin part. Other scripts are not checked.
- A final newline or several lines alone do not tag a copy, because copying a line from an editor often ends in a newline; the preview of a tagged copy mentions them, and "Paste safely" always removes the final newline.
- "Paste safely" turns every carriage return into a newline, and keeps dashes and curly quotes as they are. The preview of a tagged copy points out curly quotes and a look-alike dash (en dash, em dash, minus sign) right before an option, which a shell would not read as quotes or as an option.
- Paste safely hints are skipped for text over 256 KB; the row shows its subtitle and the action still works.
- Items over 256 KB are not looked at by detectors.
readmes.dev.yabbistir.snippets:
# Snippets

Canned replies, signatures, pull request templates and support answers as a column in yabbistir's panel, read from one plain Markdown file. Because it is just a file, a team can share it in a git repository or in iCloud Drive. ↵ pastes the snippet you pick, with `{date}`, `{time}` and more filled in, and ⌘C copies it instead.

## Example

Save this as `snippets.md` in a folder:

````markdown
Anything before the first heading is ignored, so a note to yourself can go here.

# Replies

## Thanks
Hi,

Thank you for writing in! We will answer within a day.

{weekday}, {date}

## Signature
Deniz
Support team

# Dev

## PR template
**Summary**

**How to test**

Date: {date}

## Code sample
```js
// A "## heading" inside a fence is just text.
const braces = {{ literal }};
```
````

In Settings › Extensions › Snippets, choose that folder. The panel gets a *Snippets* column with four rows, such as *Thanks* with `Replies · Hi,` underneath. Type `sig` to find *Signature* and press ↵.

## The file

- Every `## Title` line starts a snippet. Its body runs until the next `##` or `#` heading.
- An optional `# Group` line names the snippets after it. The group is shown in front of the preview in the row's second line, so searching for a group name finds its snippets.
- Fenced code blocks (three or more backticks or tildes) are kept as they are, and a `##` inside one is not a heading. Placeholders and `{{`/`}}` are still filled inside a fence, so write `{{{{` for a literal `{{` in code. A fence that is never closed swallows the rest of the file, hiding the snippets after it.
- Only `#` and `##` followed by a space are headings; `###` and deeper lines are ordinary body text. Closing hashes (`## Title ##`) are dropped from the title.
- Blank lines at the start and end of a body are trimmed; everything else is pasted exactly as written. A `#` or `##` without a space after it (`#hashtag`) is ordinary text.
- A snippet with an empty body is left out, since there would be nothing to paste. Text before the first heading, and between a `# Group` line and the first `##` after it, is ignored. Windows (CRLF) line endings are fine.
- Rows are identified by their group and title, so renaming a snippet or moving it to another group makes it a new row; editing its body does not. Two snippets with the same title in the same group stay separate rows.
- The file is read again every time the panel opens and every time you paste, so an edit shows at once. A few thousand snippets list in a fraction of a second.

## Placeholders

| Write | Pasted |
|---|---|
| `{date}` | Today's date, in the app's language: *November 4, 2026* or *4 Kasım 2026* |
| `{time}` | The time: *9:05 AM* or *09:05* |
| `{datetime}` | Both |
| `{weekday}` | The day's name: *Wednesday* or *Çarşamba* |
| `{{` and `}}` | A literal `{` and `}` |

Any other `{name}` stays as written, so code and templates with braces are safe.

## Setup

1. Create `snippets.md` (or any name) in a folder you want to use, for example in iCloud Drive or a git repository.
2. Open Settings › Extensions › Snippets and choose the folder. If the file has another name, set it under *File name*.

Until then the column says what is missing: *Choose a folder*, *There is no snippets.md in that folder*, or *snippets.md has no snippets yet*.

## Permissions and privacy

- **None.** The extension has no permissions at all. It reads the file only because you chose its folder in Settings, only inside that folder, and never writes. The file name must be a plain name (no `/`).
- The rows live in yabbistir's memory only; the extension keeps nothing between calls.

## Limits

- Only the date and time placeholders above exist; there is no cursor marker.
- A snippet pastes as plain text.
- The extension never edits the file; use any editor.
readmes.dev.yabbistir.ai-writing:
# AI Writing

Ten actions for copied text, written by Apple Intelligence, the on-device model. The text never leaves your Mac.

| Action | Offered on | What it pastes |
|---|---|---|
| Fix spelling and grammar | Text | The same text with its mistakes corrected, and nothing else changed |
| Make shorter | Text | About half as long, with the facts kept |
| Make more formal | Text | The same message in a polite, professional tone |
| Make friendlier | Text | The same message in a warmer, more casual tone |
| Turn into bullet points | Text | One idea per line, each starting with `- ` |
| Extract action items | Text | A checklist: `- [ ] Ada: send the draft by Friday` |
| Draft a reply | Text | A short reply to the message, in its tone |
| Explain this | Text and code | A plain-words explanation, at most about 150 words |
| Write a commit message | A copied diff | A Conventional Commits message |
| Write a PR description | A copied diff | `## Summary` and `## Changes` in Markdown |

Rewrites answer in the language of the text, and never translate it: that is what [Translate](../dev.yabbistir.translate) is for. Translation and summaries are not repeated here.

## Examples

Copy `can u send me the report before the meting tmrw`, press ⇧⌘V, press ⇧ on the item and choose *Fix spelling and grammar*. It pastes:

```text
Can you send me the report before the meeting tomorrow?
```

Copy the output of `git diff --staged` and choose *Write a commit message*:

```text
fix(upload): retry a failed request up to three times

A short network drop no longer fails the whole upload: the client
retries with a growing pause between tries.
```

## Short text at once, long text as a job

An action has 10 seconds, and rewriting a long text takes the model longer than that. So:

- **Fix, Make shorter, Make more formal, Make friendlier, Bullet points, Action items and Draft a reply** come in two forms, and the panel offers only the one that fits the item:
  - **Up to 400 characters** (a chat message, a short mail), the action runs at once and pastes, like any other. In Chinese, Japanese, Korean or Thai, where a character takes the model about as long as a short English word, that is fewer than 150 of those characters.
  - **Longer text** runs as a job. The panel closes, and a card under the menu bar icon shows the progress ("2 / 5 parts") with a button to cancel. When it is done, the result is pasted if the app you started from is still in front; otherwise it is on the clipboard.
- **Explain this, Write a commit message and Write a PR description** always run as jobs: an explanation or a description is as long for one line as for a page.

Characters are counted on the trimmed text, as the app counts them: some emoji, such as a flag or a thumbs-up with a skin tone, count as two or more.

On a Mac with an M4 Pro chip, each of the seven at-once actions answered a text at that limit in 0.3 to 2.3 seconds, in English, Turkish, Chinese and eleven other languages. A slower Mac takes longer, and the 8.5-second notice below covers the rest.

The panel shows one row for each task. Settings → Extensions lists every command, so the seven tasks with two forms appear there twice, with the same title. When you make one of them your ⇧↵ default, it is the default for that form only: for text up to 400 characters, or for longer text, depending on the item you set it on. Set it on a short and on a long item to have it for both.

## Long texts

The model reads a few thousand words at most, so a long text is prepared first:

- **Fix, Make shorter, Make more formal, Make friendlier, Bullet points, Action items** work part by part. The text is cut at paragraph breaks, then at sentence ends, then between words, and each part is rewritten on its own; the line breaks between parts are kept as they were. Action items from all parts make one checklist, without repeats. These take up to 40,000 characters (about 6,000 words); a longer text is refused with a notice, never cut.
- **Draft a reply** reads the newest message of a copied mail thread: it stops at a line such as `On Mon, 3 May 2026, Ada wrote:` (also when the mail wrapped it over two lines), the Turkish Apple Mail line, `-----Original Message-----` or a mail client's `From:` / `Sent:` header, and leaves out lines quoted with `>`. A text still longer than 5,000 characters keeps its start and its end.
- **Explain this** keeps the start and the end of a text longer than 5,000 characters.
- **Commit message and PR description** get a condensed diff of at most 6,000 characters: a list of the files with their added and removed lines, then the changes. Lock files (`package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, `Cargo.lock` and others), minified files and binaries are counted but not shown. Context lines go first when the diff is too long, then each file keeps an even share of the room. Lines over 300 characters are cut. A diff from `git diff`, `diff -u` or `svn diff` works, with one file or many.

The model holds about 4,096 tokens at a time, shared by its instructions, the text and the answer. A token is about three or four characters of English, fewer of most other languages, and about one character of Chinese, Japanese or Korean. So the parts are measured in tokens as well as characters: a text in those languages is cut into shorter parts, and every answer has room to be a quarter longer than its part. If a fix, a shorter text or a new tone still comes back cut short, nothing is pasted and a notice says so, rather than pasting the text without its end. An answer counts as cut short when it is far shorter than its part, or when it is shorter and stops in the middle of a sentence where its part ends one.

## Languages

- Rewrites, lists, replies and explanations of text are in the text's own language. The extension names that language to the model, because the model answers in the language of its instructions otherwise: asked only to keep "the same language as the text", it rewrote German, French, Spanish, Dutch, Japanese, Korean and Chinese texts in English when asked for a formal or a friendly tone. Named, it kept every one.
- Every language Apple Intelligence speaks on macOS 26 is recognized: Chinese, Japanese and Korean by their script, Vietnamese by its letters, and English, Turkish, German, Dutch, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Swedish, Danish and Norwegian by their common words and letters. When two are about as likely, as Danish and Norwegian often are, both are named, and the model keeps whichever it is. Chinese keeps its simplified or traditional characters.
- A language is named only when the text clearly is in it: a German or Dutch text is not taken for English, nor an Azerbaijani one for Turkish, nor a Catalan one for Spanish, because naming the wrong language would have the model translate your text. Then the model is asked to keep the text's own language.
- *Explain this* on code answers in the app's language, also when the code was copied as text.
- Commit messages and PR descriptions are in English, the convention for both.

## What is cleaned from the answer

A small model sometimes wraps its answer. Before pasting, the extension takes off a code fence around the whole answer, quotes around all of it, a first line such as "Here is the corrected text:" or "İşte düzeltilmiş metin:", and the markers the text was sent in. Each is kept when your own text had it, and a first line that rewrites your own ("Here are my thoughts:" for your "my thoughts:") stays.

- Bullet points become `- ` lines, numbered or not; action items become `- [ ] ` lines.
- A commit message's subject is at most 72 characters, with its type in lower case and no full stop, and its first verb in the imperative ("Added retry logic" becomes "add retry logic"). A `feat` that only fixes becomes `fix`, and a change to documentation or tests alone becomes `docs` or `test`. The body is wrapped at 72 characters, without lines that only repeat what the diff adds and without code blocks.
- A rewrite loses a signature the model added at its end, such as "Best regards," over "[Your Name]", when your text had none. A reply keeps its placeholders: they mark what only you can fill in.
- Square brackets the model escaped (`\[name]`) are made plain again, unless your text has backslashes of its own.
- A PR description's "Summary:" and "Changes:" become `## Summary` and `## Changes`.
- When the answer is the model declining ("I'm sorry, but I can't help with that") and has nothing to do with your text, nothing is pasted and a notice says so. A rewrite of your own "sorry, I can't make it" is a rewrite, and is pasted.
- When *Fix* gives back your text exactly as it was, the notice says "No mistakes found." A fix of only a capital letter or a full stop is a fix, and is pasted.

## When Apple Intelligence can't answer

Apple Intelligence must be turned on in System Settings, on a Mac that supports it, in a language it supports.

- The action that runs at once shows the app's own message as a notice ("Apple Intelligence is turned off…"). It does not fail: a failed action counts toward turning an extension off, and this is not the extension's fault. If the model takes more than 8.5 seconds, a notice says so, before the 10-second limit.
- A job fails on its card, with the app's own message.
- Cancelling a job stops it at once.

## Permissions

None. The on-device model is a service of the app itself: the extension needs no network, runs no programs and reads no history.

## Privacy

Your text goes only to the on-device model, and only when you choose an action. It is never logged and never put in a notice. It goes into the model's prompt between markers it cannot close, never into the instructions: Apple's model obeys its instructions over the prompt, so text placed there could steer it.

## Limits

- The on-device model is small. It can miss a mistake, misread a tone or describe a diff loosely. Read the result before you send it.
- Parts of a long text are rewritten one by one, so the tone can shift a little from one part to the next.
- The seven tasks with two forms are listed twice in Settings, and a ⇧↵ default applies to one form (see above).
- Languages are told apart by their common words and letters. A very short text in a language other than English or Turkish, such as a one-line Swedish question, may get no language named; the model is then asked to keep the text's own, and a change of tone can come back in English. A text that mixes two languages evenly gets both named.
- A rewrite that stops early right at the end of a sentence, and is not far shorter than its part, can't be told from a finished one.
- A diff is recognized by a `diff --git` line or a hunk header (`@@ -12,7 +12,8 @@`) at the start of a line, within its first 4,000 characters.
- A commit subject the model writes longer than 72 characters is cut between words.
- Needs yabbistir 0.4.0 or later.

## Sources

- Apple, [TN3193: Managing the on-device foundation model's context window](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3193-managing-the-on-device-foundation-model-s-context-window): the 4,096-token context shared by instructions, prompt and answer; about three to four characters a token in English and about one in Chinese, Japanese and Korean; splitting a large task into several calls; why a tight answer limit can cut an answer short.
- Apple, [Improving the safety of generative model output](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundationmodels/improving-the-safety-of-generative-model-output): instructions take precedence over the prompt, so untrusted text stays out of them.
- Apple, [Supporting languages and locales with Foundation Models](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundationmodels/supporting-languages-and-locales-with-foundation-models): the model answers in the language of its input; the exact phrase "The person's locale is tr_TR."; "You MUST respond in …".
- [Conventional Commits 1.0.0](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/): the `type(scope): description` form, `!` for a breaking change, and the types it names.

The word lists in `src/language.ts` and `src/words.ts`, and the list of lock files in `src/diff.ts`, are written for this extension.

## Develop

```sh
npm test -- dev.yabbistir.ai-writing          # the tests, against the fake host
npm run build -- dev.yabbistir.ai-writing     # build, check and pack dist/dev.yabbistir.ai-writing-1.0.0.yabext
npm run dev -- dev.yabbistir.ai-writing       # build, link into yabbistir and rebuild on every change
```

# Translate

Two actions for text items, both on this Mac:

- **Translate** to Turkish or English with the system's translation. The source language is detected for you. If the text is already in the target language, you are told so instead of getting a copy back.
- **Summarize** in at most three sentences with Apple Intelligence. Long text is cut to 6,000 characters first, on a character boundary.

If translation or the on-device model is not available (a missing language pack, Apple Intelligence turned off), the app's own message is shown unchanged.

None. Translation and summarizing are services of the app itself, so the extension needs no network and runs no programs.

# QR Code

Two actions, both on this Mac:

- **Show as QR code** on text and links. The QR code is an image: ↵ pastes it, ⌘C copies it. Pick its size (256, 512 or 1024 pixels) in the extension's settings; the default is 512.
- **Read QR code** on images. The text of the code comes back; if the image holds several codes, one per line. If there is no code, you are told so.

Example: copy `https://example.com/menu`, pick Show as QR code, paste the image into a slide, scan it with a phone.

## Permissions

None. The code is drawn and read by the app itself (Vision on this Mac). Nothing is sent anywhere and no program is run, so there are no tools to install.

## Limits

- A QR code holds at most roughly 2,300 to 2,950 bytes of text, depending on the encoder (less for non-Latin letters, which take 2 to 4 bytes each). Longer text gets a message instead of an image.
- Wi-Fi codes (`WIFI:S:…;T:…;P:…;;`) are returned as the text they hold, with no special handling. They contain the password: treat the result like one.
- Barcodes that Vision reads are returned the same way as QR codes.

## A word on 2FA codes

A QR code that starts with `otpauth://` or `otpauth-migration://` holds a two-factor secret. Reading it works, but the text then passes through the clipboard and lands in the clipboard history. The Secret Guard extension is meant for items like this; install it if you use it, and delete the item once you have imported it.
readmes.dev.yabbistir.symbols:
# Symbols

Two columns in yabbistir's panel for the characters that are hard to type: **Symbols** and **Kaomoji**. Nothing to install, no permissions.

## Symbols

About 350 rows in groups: Mac keys (⌘ ⌥ ⇧ ⌃ ⏎ ⌫), arrows, typography (quotes, dashes, the ellipsis, bullets, primes and the spaces), math, currency (including ₺ and €), check marks and stars, Greek letters, superscripts and subscripts, fractions, box drawing and the legal marks (© ® ™ § ¶ °).

A row's title is the symbol and its subtitle is its name in the app's language, the same name in the other language (when it differs) and its code point, such as *Command · U+2318* or *Türk lirası · Turkish lira · U+20BA*. The panel's search looks at all of it, so typing `lira`, `lirası`, `command` or `2318` finds it in either language. Characters that show as nothing, such as the non-breaking space, the zero-width space or the soft hyphen, have their name in square brackets as the title.

- ↵ pastes the symbol, ⌘C copies it.
- ⇧↵ pastes its HTML form: the entity's name where the HTML standard has one (`©`, `—`, `α`), the numeric form otherwise (`⌘`).

## Kaomoji

About 160 rows in twelve groups: happy, love, sad, angry, surprised, shrug, table flip, bear, cat, music, sleepy and greeting. A row's title is the kaomoji and its subtitle is the group and a few search words in both languages.

- ↵ pastes the kaomoji, ⌘C copies it.
- ⇧↵ pastes it for Markdown: a backslash, an underscore, an asterisk, a backtick and a tilde get a backslash in front, so `¯\_(ツ)_/¯` survives as `¯\\\_(ツ)\_/¯` and a `~~` cannot strike text through.

## Example

Open the panel, move to the *Symbols* column and type `euro`: ↵ pastes €, ⇧↵ pastes `€`. In the *Kaomoji* column, type `shrug` and press ↵.

## Permissions and tools

None. The extension needs no permission and no command-line tool: both columns are tables inside the extension. It reads nothing from your Mac, uses no network, stores nothing and writes nothing to the log.

## Limits

- A space can't be pasted from a column: yabbistir treats a value of white space only as empty. ↵ on the non-breaking, en, em, thin and narrow spaces says so, and ⇧↵ pastes their HTML form (` `). The zero-width space and joiner and the soft hyphen paste as they are.
- Names and search words are in English and Turkish only; any other app language reads English.
- Row ids are the code points (`u-2318`) and, for kaomoji, the group and the place in it (`shrug-1`). New kaomoji are added at the end of a group so the ids stay.

## Where the data comes from

The symbols are Unicode facts: characters and their code points, named by hand in English and Turkish after the Unicode character names. Unicode data is free to use ([Unicode License v3](https://www.unicode.org/license.txt)). The HTML entity names are the ones in the [HTML Standard's list of named character references](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/named-characters.html) (CC0-licensed). The kaomoji are short public strings and the search words are written for this extension. The code is MIT-licensed.
